entry.title: A complete addition formula for twisted Edwards curves, a cryptographic curve family
entry.summary: Complete Addition Law for Twisted Edwards Curves IACR ePrint · Nov 2, 2026The paper constructs complete addition formulas in extended coordinates for twisted Edwards curves, valid for every pair of rational points under specified conditions. It analyses the exceptional fibres using a difference morphism and gives full and mixed evaluation schedules. The authors compare operation costs across cases, and state that doubling cost does not depend on the choice of coefficient. ★★★★ Notable: The authors construct complete addition laws for twisted Edwards curves, characterize exceptional fibres, prove existence over odd finite fields, and report operation costs.

entry.title: Communication complexity of secure MPC from a random oracle, including quantum variants
entry.summary: On the (Quantum) Communication Complexity of Secure MPC from a Random Oracle IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies the communication complexity of information-theoretically secure multi-party computation when only symmetric-key assumptions are available, modeled as a random oracle. For MPC with preprocessing, the authors prove that the known lower bound still holds in this model, so a random oracle cannot reduce online communication. For honest-majority MPC they give an Ω(|C|) lower bound and a matching construction for degree-2 polynomials, including inner products, when n = O(log λ). The paper also analyzes protocols that use quantum communication or a quantum-accessible random oracle. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend MPC communication lower bounds to the random oracle model, match them with a degree-2 construction, and study quantum communication savings and their costs.

entry.title: Tight depth lower bounds for amplifying pseudorandom generator stretch
entry.summary: Tight Depth Lower Bounds for Stretch Amplification IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026The paper studies the depth overhead of stretch amplification for pseudorandom generators in the black-box model. It shows that black-box constructions with d adaptive phases satisfy an upper bound on output length M, implying the standard repeated-composition amplification is essentially optimal. The results also yield tight depth lower bounds for black-box PRF constructions from PRGs. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give tight depth lower bounds for black-box stretch amplification of PRGs, extending to PRFs, Avoid, and an oracle separation.

entry.title: Recovering master keys from the WBSLT white-box AES design by quotienting redundant lookup tables
entry.summary: Quotienting Redundant Tables: Practical Master-Key Recovery from WBSLT White-Box AES IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026This paper is a cryptanalysis of WBSLT, a white-box AES design presented at NDSS 2026. It shows that the joint output of first-round TypeII lookup tables has an exact 16 × 16 quotient, which reveals the nibble partition of each AES input byte. Using public tables and traces of chosen encoded inputs, the authors report recovering the master key in the tested instances. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors use an exact quotient of public lookup tables to recover WBSLT white-box AES master keys, reporting full recovery across 200 general instances and variants.

entry.title: Cryptanalysis of MinRank 2.0: Reassessing Attacks on the MinRank Problem
entry.summary: Cryptanalysis of MinRank 2.0 IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026This paper revisits attacks on MinRank, the hard problem underlying several post-quantum schemes such as the Mirath signature and multivariate schemes like UOV and MAYO. The authors improve the kernel-search attack, lowering its cost by 3 to 6 bits on Mirath parameters and solving Courtois challenge D, open since 2001. They also show that existing complexity estimates for the Kipnis–Shamir attack are inaccurate and give corrected figures. Finally, they extend the Support-Minors and Minors modelings with field equations, which lowers their estimates over small fields. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors improve kernel-search MinRank attacks, report solving open Courtois challenge D, and correct Kipnis-Shamir complexity estimates affecting several post-quantum schemes.

entry.title: The Fairest of Them All: Fair Leader Election Secure Under Two Corruption Models
entry.summary: The Fairest of Them All: Best-of-Both-Worlds Fair Leader Election IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies how to pick a random leader fairly from n parties. It introduces best-of-both-worlds (BoBW) fairness: a small number of corrupt parties cannot bias the result, and a larger number still cannot improve their collective chances or reduce any honest party's chances. The authors present a protocol for t_S + t_GT < n, prove it optimal via a generalization of Cleve's impossibility, and give a protocol for the perfect-security setting. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a new best-of-both-worlds fairness notion, give a protocol, and report a matching optimality proof with a generalized Cleve impossibility.

entry.title: Leakage-tolerant secure computation without leakage-free setup
entry.summary: Leakage-Tolerant Computation without Leakage-Free Setup IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies leakage-tolerant multi-party computation, where leakage from honest parties' internal states reveals no more than their inputs and outputs already do. In a computational model assuming only augmented non-committing encryption, the authors show that every adaptively well-formed functionality admits a semi-honest leakage-tolerant protocol without leakage-free preprocessing or a common reference string. Under the decisional Diffie-Hellman assumption, this extends to malicious security in the CRS model for all deterministic functionalities. In the information-theoretic setting, secure erasure enables statistically secure protocols for arbitrary functionalities when fewer than half the participants are maliciously corrupted. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show semi-honest leakage-tolerant MPC from augmented non-committing encryption alone, without leakage-free preprocessing or CRS, plus information-theoretic results and impossibilities.

entry.title: Keeping secrets safe from physical leaks by refreshing matrices
entry.summary: Leakage-Resilient Computation via Matrix Refreshing IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies how to protect secret data from side-channel attacks, where a device leaks partial information about its internal state. The secret is split into two vectors held by separate parts of the implementation, and it is refreshed by multiplying one share by a uniform invertible matrix and the other by its inverse. The authors prove this refresh remains secure under continual local leakage and give bounds on statistical distance. They also present a Boolean-circuit compiler with a privacy error bound, and formalize these results in Lean 4. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a matrix-refresh scheme for two-party shares with a statistical bound under continual local leakage, plus a circuit compiler.

entry.title: The Cost of Agreement in Secure Multiparty Computation
entry.summary: The Price of Agreement in Secure Multiparty Computation IACR ePrint · Nov 4, 2026This paper studies secure multiparty computation (MPC) when a dishonest majority of parties may be corrupted, where output delivery cannot be guaranteed and protocols settle for security with abort. It focuses on unanimous abort, where either all honest parties receive output or all abort. The authors prove that for t ≤ n−2 corruptions, unanimous-abort broadcast and hence UA-MPC require at least t/(2(n−t)) rounds in expectation, matching the asymptotic bound for broadcast without abort. Consequently, expected-constant-round UA-MPC is possible if and only if a constant fraction of parties is honest. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors prove UA-broadcast and UA-MPC need at least t/(2(n-t)) expected rounds, answering an open question with a tight bound matching Dolev-Strong.

entry.title: Differential Cryptanalysis of SPEEDY: Revised Security Evaluation and Improved Key Recovery
entry.summary: Differential Cryptanalysis of SPEEDY: Revised Security Evaluation and Improved Key Recovery Attack IACR ePrint · Nov 4, 2026This paper re-evaluates the resistance of the low-latency block cipher SPEEDY against differential cryptanalysis. The authors propose a search method based on search patterns that imposes no structural restrictions, using computational pruning and a conservative evaluation over the global space. For 4 rounds, the minimum number of active S-boxes is narrowed to [33,34], and the highest-probability differential characteristics known for 2 to 5 rounds are presented. The authors also optimize a prior key recovery attack, yielding the best known attack on SPEEDY-7-192. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a search-pattern method removing structural restrictions, improving bounds and reporting stronger characteristics and a key recovery attack on SPEEDY.

entry.title: Hardness of TFNP Classes in the Random Oracle Model
entry.summary: TFNP in the Random Oracle Model IACR ePrint · Nov 4, 2026This paper examines which major TFNP classes are hard in the random oracle model. It shows that PPAD is hard on average in this setting, which together with known PLS hardness yields average-case hardness for EoPL. It also shows that UEoPL can be solved with polynomially many queries by an unbounded solver, and begins studying separations between TFNP subclasses. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors prove PPAD is average-case hard in the random oracle model, resolving a long-standing open problem and separating EoPL from UEoPL.

entry.title: Information Loss Is All You Need: Post-quantum pseudorandomness in TC⁰ from worst-case lattice hardness
entry.summary: Information Loss Is All You Need: TC⁰ Pseudorandomness from Worst-Case Lattices IACR ePrint · Nov 4, 2026The paper introduces the learning with algebraic rounding (LAR) assumption, which replaces LWE's random noise with an explicit deterministic integer rounding map. Its pseudorandomness is based on quantum worst-case lattice problems such as GapSVP and SIVP. The authors use this to construct the first post-quantum weak pseudorandom function with joint key-and-input evaluation in TC⁰. They also show hardness of learning two-hidden-layer ReLU networks from noiseless uniform random examples. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a learning-with-algebraic-rounding assumption, derive a post-quantum TC⁰ weak PRF from worst-case lattice hardness, and report hardness for learning two-hidden-layer ReLU networks.

entry.title: Power-analysis attack study on SHA-2-based SLH-DSA signatures
entry.summary: Correlation Power Analysis on SHA-2-Based SLH-DSA IACR ePrint · Nov 4, 2026This paper applies non-profiled correlation power analysis to the address-based pseudorandom function of SLH-DSA across all six SHA-2 parameter sets, targeting SHA-256 compression rounds and message-schedule expansion. Experiments on an STM32F303 ARM Cortex-M4 used 30 secret seeds with 5,000 power traces per seed. Reported rates are conditional stage-wise results with preceding secret values supplied correctly, not end-to-end seed recovery rates. The authors conclude that side-channel protection must cover both compression rounds and message-schedule expansion. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a staged non-profiled correlation power attack on SHA-2 SLH-DSA, covering compression rounds and message schedule, evaluated on an STM32F303 Cortex-M4.

entry.title: Provable fast algorithms for exact shortest vector and approximate closest vector problems on random q-ary lattices
entry.summary: Fast Provable Algorithms for Approximate CVP and Exact SVP on Random q-ary Lattices IACR ePrint · Nov 1, 2026This paper presents provable randomized algorithms for the exact shortest vector problem (SVP) and the 5/3-approximate closest vector problem (CVP) in the Euclidean norm on random q-ary lattices, for any integer modulus q. The approach adapts the Howgrave-Graham–Joux representation method to find short ternary solutions of random linear congruences. For density at most 1, both algorithms' time exponents fall below the heuristic sieving exponent of 0.2925. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend the Howgrave-Graham–Joux representation method to all integer moduli, giving provable SVP and CVP algorithms on random q-ary lattices with time exponents below sieving.

entry.title: A Compiler Keeping Computations Secure Under Constant Continual Memory Leakage
entry.summary: A Constant-Rate Compiler for Continual Memory Leakage IACR ePrint · Nov 2, 2026This paper presents a compiler that transforms any deterministic computation so that physical leakage from its implementation reveals nothing beyond its input-output behaviour, under the continual memory leakage model. It achieves constant leakage-rate, whereas previous general compilers tolerated only inverse-polynomial leakage-rate. Applied to decryption of IND-CCA2 secure public-key encryption, it yields IND-CCLA2 security, instantiated from LWE and LPN, and the authors also obtain signatures, PRFs and MACs via a generalization. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a constant-leakage-rate compiler in the continual memory leakage model, improving prior inverse-polynomial rates, with applications to PKE, signatures and PRFs.

entry.title: Tightly Secure Unique Signatures in the Random Oracle Model via Hash-and-Subset-Sign
entry.summary: Unique Signature Schemes with Tight Security in the Random Oracle Model via Hash-and-Subset-Sign IACR ePrint · Nov 2, 2026This paper studies unique signature schemes, in which each message has exactly one valid signature. Most such schemes previously suffered a security loss at least linear in the number of signature queries under EUF-CMA security. The authors give a hash-and-sign-like general transformation that turns a scheme with weaker security into an EUF-CMA secure one. The result is the first tightly secure unique signature scheme with verifiable public keys that needs only a constant number (six) of random oracle queries to sign and verify. The paper also gives two tightly secure constructions in the multi-user setting. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a hash-and-subset-sign transformation yielding the first tight unique signature with verifiable keys using constant oracle queries, plus multi-user constructions.

entry.title: Beyond Standard Indifferentiability: Simulator Properties for Fiat-Shamir Security
entry.summary: Beyond Standard Indifferentiability: Simulator Properties for Fiat-Shamir Security IACR ePrint · Oct 31, 2026This paper studies how to replace the random oracle in the Fiat-Shamir transform with structured hash constructions while preserving security. It shows that standard indifferentiability can still serve as the oracle-replacement abstraction, giving generic transfer theorems for three knowledge-soundness extraction interfaces. It also argues that the reconstruction requirement for rewinding extraction is inherent, and instantiates the framework for tagged prefix-free Merkle-Damgard and a fixed-output permutation sponge. ★★★★ Notable: Addresses the Chiesa-Orru gap by showing standard indifferentiability suffices as an oracle-replacement abstraction, with generic transfer theorems and a rewinding-reconstruction lower bound under dis

entry.title: Hidden Curves and Short Duals: Limits of Masked-Code Encryption
entry.summary: Hidden Curves and Short Duals: Cubic Jets, Dual Leaks, and the Limits of Masked-Code Encryption IACR ePrint · Nov 1, 2026This paper analyzes two masking schemes, Wang's RLCE and the (U|U+V) construction of UVW-KEM, which were proposed as compact alternatives to Goppa codes. The authors show that for Reed-Solomon and algebraic-geometry codes the mask hides a curve, which can be detected through cubic jet counts, and they explain a public-key key recovery attack on UVW-KEM that is not specific to UVW. They also show that both masks preserve the dual of the hidden code, leaking low-weight dual words. The authors conclude that no compact masked trapdoor code is currently known that avoids these structural weaknesses. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors propose hidden-pairing codes, give a closed-form cubic jet dependency bound, and report that both masks leak the hidden code's dual across parameters.

entry.title: Auditing Multi-Proxy Explanations of Web User Preferences: Identification Boundaries and Abstention
entry.summary: Auditing Multi-Proxy Explanations of Web User Preferences: Identification Boundaries and Abstention arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies how explanations of proxies used to infer web user preferences, such as behavior, ratings, text, or LLM-generated profiles, may reflect measurement processes rather than the true preferences. It proposes an audit framework that distinguishes point identification, partial identification, and abstention, and shows that when a strict majority of uncontaminated proxy attributions hold under feature-dependent, arbitrarily signed bias, a coordinatewise median can recover latent attribution support and direction. In an Amazon study, median aggregation reduced conditional sign error, but weak comparator calibration limits the evidence to alignment with the fitted surface rather than latent-preference recovery. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present a multi-proxy audit framework, prove a sharp strict-majority threshold, and report results on a known-truth benchmark and an Amazon study relevant to auditing user preferences.

entry.title: Balanced Fair Division and Generalized Kneser Graphs
entry.summary: Balanced Fair Division and Generalized Kneser Graphs arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper studies allocating indivisible goods to two prescribed nonempty groups whose members have arbitrary monotone valuations. It guarantees balanced envy-freeness up to one good (EF1) for up to five agents and up to two goods (EF2) for up to nine agents. These results follow from chromatic bounds for generalized Kneser graphs KG(2n,n,r). The authors also resolve a conjecture of Jafari and Alipour and improve known bounds on the chromatic number for r=3. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report EF1 guarantees for up to five agents and EF2 for up to nine in balanced division of indivisible goods, and state that the chromatic number of generalized Kneser graph KG(2n,n,2) is

entry.title: TxBench: A Benchmark of Attack Transactions and Evidence-Backed Negatives on Seven EVM Chains
entry.summary: TxBench: A Benchmark of Attack Transactions and Evidence-Backed Negatives on Seven EVM Chains arXiv · Nov 3, 2026TxBench is a benchmark for testing detectors of malicious smart-contract transactions, covering seven EVM chains. Its attack transactions come from cited incidents in BlockSec's library and the EVM Hack Registry, filtered by a five-step pipeline that rebuilds each transaction's execution, and its negatives are ordinary chain transactions confirmed as legitimate. Of 1,850 cited transactions, 1,012 attacks from 602 incidents were accepted. Four zero-shot LLMs were precise but detected at most 0.43 of the attacks and no key compromises. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present a benchmark of EVM attack transactions labeled by their own execution, with evidence-backed negatives; the summary reports 1,012 accepted attacks from 1,850 cited transactions, che

entry.title: Operational thresholds for long-range entanglement in quantum networks
entry.summary: Operational Thresholds for Long-Range Entanglement in Quantum Networks arXiv · Nov 4, 2026Quantum networks share entanglement between distant nodes by chaining short entangled links with local operations that succeed only probabilistically. The paper uses a stochastic extension of concurrence percolation on hierarchical (U,V)-flower networks to derive an exact recursion for end-to-end survival probability. For the (2,2)-flower it gives a closed-form phase boundary, and it finds a second threshold in initial link quality. The results show operational reliability and link quality can compensate each other.` ★★★★ Notable: The authors incorporate probabilistic local operations into percolation theory, deriving an analytical phase boundary on hierarchical flower networks; results are reported only for specific network fa

entry.title: Improved Code Rate and Distance for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Gates
entry.summary: Substantially Improved Rate and Distance for Addressable Transversal Phase Gates arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies quantum error-correcting codes that allow fully addressable transversal phase gates, a key ingredient for fault-tolerant quantum computation. Using a cyclic encoding beyond the binary CSS framework, the authors substantially improve lower bounds on rate and relative distance at every fixed Clifford hierarchy level h≥3. They present a deterministic polynomial-time algebraic-geometric construction and an exponential-time counting construction with exact verification, the latter improving the bound by roughly 2.86 times. The paper also gives an upper bound for such codes and constructs examples with 48 and 90 physical qubits supporting transversal T gates. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use cyclic encoding beyond binary CSS to improve rate and distance bounds for addressable transversal phase gates, with polynomial-time construction.

entry.title: Autonomous cooling of Kerr-cat qubits extends bit-flip times to minutes
entry.summary: Autonomous cooling of Kerr-cat qubits to minutes-long bit-flip times arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies Kerr-cat qubits built from superconducting oscillators, whose bit-flip times are normally limited by excitations causing interwell switching. The authors show that the nonlinear interaction that confines the states can also cool these excitations by transferring them to a lossy readout mode. This raises bit-flip times to 450 seconds while retaining fast coherent control. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors use the nonlinear confinement interaction for autonomous cooling, reporting minutes-long bit-flip times verified by spectroscopy and relaxation measurements on superconducting oscillators.

entry.title: Real-time analysis of the Yukawa-SYK model in closed and open systems
entry.summary: Closed- and open-system characterization of the Yukawa-SYK model in real time arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies the Yukawa-SYK model, in which bosons and fermions interact through random all-to-all couplings that drive the boson to criticality without fine tuning. Using the Schwinger-Keldysh formalism, the authors treat closed and open systems in one framework and map phase diagrams for thermal steady states, including newly identified high-temperature regimes. They also introduce markers built from two-point functions that are accessible in linear response and require no fit of conformal exponents, along with quantum Fisher information bounds. ★★★★ Notable: The authors unify closed and open YSYK dynamics via real-time Schwinger-Keldysh, identify new high-temperature regimes and a criticality budget, and derive measurable markers and quantum Fisher inform

entry.title: A paper on random purifications of isometries and quantum channels
entry.summary: On Random Purifications of Isometries and Channels arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper studies how queries to an isometry or quantum channel can be converted into queries to a random unitary completion or a random isometry dilation. It gives an efficient simulator for sequential forward queries to a fixed Haar random unitary completion. It also shows that approximating the quantum switch to constant error below 1/2 requires exponentially many channel queries. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend random purification techniques to isometries and channels, giving a simulator, exponential query lower bounds, and an improved quantum switch result.

entry.title: Universal control of free-electron sidebands using alternating light-electron interactions and free drift.
entry.summary: Universal Free-Electron-Sideband Control arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper studies controlling the longitudinal wavefunction of free electrons using alternating photon-induced near-field electron microscopy (PINEM) interactions and free drifts. The authors prove that a finite sequence of these operations can approximate any inner-product-preserving map from a finite-dimensional input subspace into the ideal electron-sideband Hilbert space to arbitrary accuracy, a protocol they call PINEMAD. Numerical results indicate that parameter optimization enables high-fidelity state preparation at finite electron energy spreads. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove alternating PINEM interactions and free drifts approximate any inner-product-preserving map, and report numerical high-fidelity state preparation.

entry.title: PolicyIK: Reinforcement Learning for Precise Robot Arm Inverse Kinematics
entry.summary: PolicyIK: High-Precision Inverse Kinematics for Robot Arms with Reinforcement Learning arXiv · Nov 4, 2026This paper presents PolicyIK, a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning policy that computes precise inverse kinematics, converting end-effector pose commands into robot joint motions. In simulation, the trained PPO policy keeps final-second mean errors within 1 mm and 0.2 degrees on 93.5% of held-out tasks, rising to 98.9% with a deployment protocol. In simulated pick-and-place, it executes end-effector commands from the π0.5 vision-language-action policy with 95.7% success. ★★★★ Notable: The authors apply RL to high-precision IK with offset and dwell rewards, reporting gains over four classical controllers in simulation and on a physical arm.

entry.title: Near-MMS fair allocations when few extra agents are present
entry.summary: Almost-MMS allocations with small agent redundancy arXiv · Nov 4, 2026The paper studies fair allocation of indivisible goods, asking whether a subset of n agents among more agents can each receive at least a fixed fraction of their n-maximin share (MMS). The authors show that when agent redundancy is positive, this fraction approaches 1 as n grows. This also holds without redundancy when the number of goods is at most (2−c)n. Adapting their techniques, they improve a result of Ezra and Garbuz, showing that without redundancy, n−O(log²n) agents can always receive their full MMS. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show that with agent redundancy the MMS fraction tends to 1 as n grows, yielding a corollary for m≤(2-c)n and improving Ezra and Garbuz's result.

entry.title: Breaking quantum query barriers for graph collision
entry.summary: Breaking the quantum barriers for Graph Collision arXiv · Nov 4, 2026The paper studies the graph collision problem, which asks whether a known graph on n vertices has an edge with both endpoints marked, accessed through queries to the marking input bits. The authors give a bounded-error quantum algorithm using Õ(n^{92/139}) queries, refuting a conjectured Ω(n^{2/3}) lower bound, and refine it to Õ(n^{11/17}) queries. They also prove an Ω(√(n log n)) quantum query lower bound, which exceeds the O(√n) certificate complexity barrier of the positive adversary method. ★★★★ Notable: The authors refute the conjectured Ω(n^{2/3}) lower bound with quantum algorithms of Õ(n^{92/139}) and Õ(n^{11/17}) queries, plus a new lower bound.

entry.title: Agnostic learning by imitating: showing discriminative and generative learning are equally hard
entry.summary: Agnostic Learning by Imitating arXiv · Nov 4, 2026The paper studies whether training a model that separates positive and negative labels as well as the best model in a class is harder or easier than training a generator whose outputs cannot be told apart from real data by any model in that class. The authors prove the two tasks are computationally equivalent, extending a previously known reduction with an efficient reduction in the opposite direction. Using adaptive queries to a multiaccuracy oracle, they achieve agnostic learning and several other learning objectives. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors prove equivalence in complexity between multiaccuracy and agnostic learning via a new efficient reduction using adaptive oracle queries and follow-the-leader techniques.

entry.title: A circuit for learning from examples inside a prompt, without updating model weights
entry.summary: A Circuit for In-Context Learning arXiv · Nov 4, 2026The paper studies how language models learn few-shot sentence classification with arbitrary labels from demonstrations in the prompt, using three 3–4B-parameter transformers. It reports that the models implement a key-value memory over label-token positions, with attention heads storing demonstration classes as keys and upper-layer heads copying matching labels at query time. Causal tests such as activation patching and head ablations support each step, and the same components also appear in a transformer trained from scratch. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a full composed circuit for in-context learning with arbitrary labels, a gated key-value memory, validated causally across models and scales.

entry.title: MedPhysBench: a benchmark testing language models on medical physics calculations and error detection
entry.summary: MedPhysBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Language Models on Medical Physics Calculations and Error Detection arXiv · Nov 4, 2026MedPhysBench is a benchmark of medical physics calculation items across radiation therapy, diagnostic imaging, nuclear medicine and radiation protection, paired with error-detection items. On 1,200 held-out test items, 12 models scored between 33.3% and 100.0% on calculation. Models also varied widely in detecting planted errors in colleagues' worksheets, and the authors release code and per-item results. ★★★★ Notable: The authors combine medical physics calculations and error detection in one benchmark, using protocol code for reference answers; they report evaluating 12 models on 1,200 held-out items.

entry.title: PyRUA-DataFarm: An LLM Agent Generating Real-Ready Robot Training Data Without Teleoperation
entry.summary: PyRUA-DataFarm: LLM Agent as a Cost-Efficient Teleoperator for Real-Ready Robot Data arXiv · Nov 4, 2026This paper presents DataFarm, in which a coding agent rebuilds a robot task in simulation from a data request and one calibration episode, writing the scene, an expert controller, and a success judge. A video model conditioned on real images renders the simulated rollouts into photorealistic multi-view video labelled with robot actions. On five real-robot tasks, policies trained only on this data matched policies trained on as many teleoperated episodes (93 vs. 84 successes in 100 trials) and performed better under an unseen tablecloth and coloured light (87 vs. 46 successes). The authors report an average adaptation cost of $21 per task and $0.80 per additional episode. ★★★★ Notable: A coding agent replaces teleoperators, generating simulated tasks rendered photorealistically; the authors report matching teleoperation success on five real-robot tasks and lower cost.

entry.title: Universal hardness certified via masking channels
entry.summary: Universal Hardness From Masking Channels arXiv · Nov 4, 2026This paper generalizes the hardcore lemma of Impagliazzo (1995) into a broad learning-theoretic framework for average-case hardness of computing functions. It develops a general method for certifying hardness that applies to non-Boolean functions and many notions of hardness beyond the 0-1 loss, using convex duality to select the appropriate fidelity measure. The authors derive multiclass generalizations and construct a universal masking channel that applies to many hardness notions simultaneously. ★★★★ Notable: The authors generalize the hardcore lemma to non-Boolean functions and convex losses via masking channels and convex duality, giving a tight characterization and a universal channel.

entry.title: Reassurance Error in AI Severe-Weather Advice Tested Against Real NWS Alerts
entry.summary: False Reassurance in LLM Severe-Weather Guidance: A Replayable Evaluation Against Real NWS Alerts arXiv · Nov 4, 2026This paper examines whether an LLM assistant that cannot see official severe-weather alerts may tell users conditions are calm while a warning is active, a failure the authors call false reassurance. They replayed 117 frozen cases built from real U.S. National Weather Service alerts through five conditions of a Claude-based preparedness pipeline. Access to real alerts removed false reassurance (paired McNemar p < 0.0001), while a blind neutral prompt produced it in 37.7% of alert cases. The authors release the dataset, labels and code. ★★★★ Notable: The authors define false reassurance and replay 117 real NWS alert cases across five prompt and alert-access conditions, releasing data and code.

entry.title: Training an AI on answers it believes are wrong can make it misaligned
entry.summary: Knowingly Wrong: Training LLMs Against Their Own Beliefs can Induce Misalignment arXiv · Nov 4, 2026The paper shows that fine-tuning a language model on data it believes to be false, even when the data has no harmful content, can cause broad misalignment. Experiments across mathematics, trivia, cooking and sports found that the more strongly the model disbelieves the training answers, the more misaligned it becomes. The authors attribute this to an inconsistency between the model's internal beliefs and its stated answers. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report that fine-tuning on believed-false but harmless data induces broad misalignment, with misaligned answers rising from 4% to over 60% in mathematics experiments.

entry.title: Conformal Prediction at Performative Equilibrium: How Deployment-Induced Data Shifts Limit Coverage Guarantees
entry.summary: Conformal Prediction at Performative Equilibrium: The Price of Performativity arXiv · Nov 4, 2026This paper studies conformal prediction when a deployed predictor changes the data distribution, requiring prediction sets to achieve coverage under the distribution at a performatively stable predictor. The authors identify a phase transition at total-variation sensitivity L=1: for L≥1 no procedure can guarantee both valid coverage and nontrivial sets, while for L<1 the minimax excess miscoverage scales as 1/((1-L)√n). A transfer theorem links approximate equilibrium predictors to coverage, and experiments including credit scoring illustrate the predicted behavior. ★★★★ Notable: The authors identify a phase transition at L=1 for conformal prediction at performative equilibrium, give minimax lower bounds and a transfer theorem, and report experiments confirming the predicted t

entry.title: Detecting Hidden Knowledge in LLMs via Activation Geometry
entry.summary: The Geometry of Ignorance: Detecting Suppressed Knowledge in LLMs through Activation Fragmentation arXiv · Nov 4, 2026This paper proposes a way to tell whether a large language model truly knows a concept by measuring the geometric coherence of anon-vectors, the hidden-state differences between a concept query and its anonymized paraphrase. Genuine knowledge forms a tight, low-entropy cluster, while ignorance causes geometric fragmentation. Across ten instruction-tuned models, these metrics reliably separate known from unknown concepts and correlate with adversarial recovery after unlearning. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose geometric fragmentation of anon-vectors to measure LLM knowledge and predict unlearning recovery, reporting validation across ten models, four attacks, and five unlearning algorith

entry.title: Gaussian partitioning: a tool for reliably learning multi-index models
entry.summary: Gaussian Partitioning for Reliable Learning of Multi-Index Models arXiv · Nov 4, 2026The paper introduces Gaussian partitioning, an algorithmic method for distributions that are smooth with respect to a Gaussian. It splits space into polyhedral regions so that nearly all probability mass lies in thin strips that constrain only a few orthogonal directions. The authors use this to build agnostic learners for several Boolean multi-index model classes, including functions of halfspaces, and also prove Statistical Query lower bounds. For functions of k halfspaces, the dimension dependence is improved over previous results. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce Gaussian partitioning and improve dimension dependence for learning multi-index models, with matching SQ lower bounds reported.

entry.title: Logarithmic regret bound for alternating mirror descent in zero-sum games
entry.summary: Logarithmic Regret for Alternating Mirror Descent arXiv · Nov 4, 2026This paper studies alternating online mirror descent (AltOMD), a learning rule for zero-sum games. The authors prove that, for two-player zero-sum bilinear games with compact convex strategy sets and mild regularity assumptions on the regularizers, the sum of both players' external regrets is O(log T), which is nearly constant. These assumptions hold for the negative entropy regularizer, so the alternating multiplicative weights update algorithm also attains logarithmic regret. The bound further implies an O(log T / T) duality gap for the averaged strategies. ★★★★ Notable: The authors resolve an open question, proving an O(log T) regret bound for alternating OMD in bilinear zero-sum games and verifying it for the negative entropy regularizer.

entry.title: Fast Equilibrium Computation for the Colonel Blotto Game
entry.summary: Efficient Equilibrium Computation in Colonel Blotto Games arXiv · Nov 4, 2026The paper studies Colonel Blotto, a resource-allocation game where two players split budgets across battlefields and the higher allocation wins each battlefield's value. It gives a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme that computes an epsilon-Nash equilibrium in time polynomial in the input length and 1/epsilon. For sufficiently balanced budgets and battlefield values, it also computes exact equilibria in linear time. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme for equilibria in Colonel Blotto games, plus linear-time exact equilibria for balanced cases.

entry.title: Differentially private agnostic learning of halfspaces with no extra sample cost
entry.summary: Privacy for Free in Efficient Agnostic Halfspace Learning arXiv · Nov 4, 2026This paper presents the first computationally efficient differentially private algorithms for agnostically learning halfspaces. It covers three settings: improper learning under Gaussian and log-concave marginals, proper learning under Gaussian marginals, and semi-agnostic learning under Gaussian marginals. In all three, the extra sample complexity caused by privacy matches the corresponding non-private sample complexity. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report the first efficient differentially private agnostic halfspace learners, with privacy adding no sample complexity beyond non-private bounds.

entry.title: Robust Reconstruction of Power Lines from Incomplete Mobile and Aerial LiDAR Data
entry.summary: Robust Reconstruction of Power Lines from Incomplete Mobile and Aerial LiDAR Data arXiv · Nov 4, 2026This paper presents an automated method for reconstructing individual power conductors from mobile and aerial LiDAR point clouds, even when returns are sparse, incomplete, or occluded by vegetation. It combines scaled density-based clustering, robust polynomial fitting, and iterative fragment merging, applying the same pipeline to both data types without modality-specific tuning. On the aerial dataset it reports 96.87% precision, 96.66% recall, and a 0.127 m geometric RMSE; on the mobile dataset, a 0.045 m point-to-model RMSE and 95.27% coverage. Source code and data are publicly available. ★★★★ Notable: The authors apply one modality-agnostic pipeline to mobile and aerial LiDAR power-line reconstruction, reporting 96.87% precision and 96.66% recall on aerial data with degradation and sensitivity expe

entry.title: From Natural to Medical Images: Whether Diffusion Models Transfer to Medical Image Generation
entry.summary: From Natural Images to Medical Scans: Transferability of Diffusion Models for Medical Image Generation arXiv · Nov 4, 2026This paper examines whether diffusion denoisers pretrained on natural images transfer to medical image generation. Experiments span latent and pixel-space paradigms, model sizes from 131M to 952M parameters, and two radiology datasets, RadImageNet and BraTS. Natural-image initialisation consistently improves generation quality, and the benefit tracks spatial structure rather than semantics. The authors conclude that natural-image denoisers transfer positively to medical ones in their setup. ★★★★ Notable: The authors systematically study natural-image transfer to medical diffusion denoisers, identify spatial structure as the key channel, and report 21-34% gFID gains on RadImageNet and BraTS.

entry.title: Provably Learning Mixtures of Linear Experts
entry.summary: Provably Learning Mixtures of Linear Experts arXiv · Nov 4, 2026This paper studies whether gradient-based training of Mixture-of-Experts models converges to good solutions. It analyzes a gated mixture with linear experts and a gate defined by Gaussian clusters in the input space, and proves that gradient EM on the likelihood jointly trains the gate and experts to any prescribed accuracy. Under logarithmic overparameterization and a separation condition on gate centers, convergence occurs in polynomially many iterations from random gate initialization and least-squares-initialized experts. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a global convergence guarantee for joint gradient EM training of gated linear-expert mixtures, with experiments on the predicted phase transition.

entry.title: RoboTryOn: Creating Robot Demonstrations from Human Videos via Virtual Try-On
entry.summary: RoboTryOn: Synthesizing Dexterous Robot Demonstrations from Human Videos via Virtual Try-On arXiv · Nov 4, 2026RoboTryOn converts human videos into videos of a target robot specified by a reference image, keeping the original task, objects, and background. It translates keyframes autoregressively for visual consistency, then synthesizes video conditioned on the human hand skeleton. An inverse dynamics model using depth features infers action labels from the synthesized videos for policy learning. Policies trained on this synthetic data raised average success on novel tasks from 2% to 60%, at about a third of teleoperation collection cost. ★★★★ Notable: The authors treat human-to-robot translation as virtual try-on, synthesizing robot videos for policy learning; the abstract reports bimanual success rising from 2% to 60%.

entry.title: Tight Bound for Randomized Truthful Scheduling
entry.summary: Tight Analysis of Randomized Truthful Scheduling: An (m+1)/2 Lower Bound arXiv · Nov 4, 2026The paper studies randomized truthful mechanisms for minimizing makespan on unrelated machines. It proves a lower bound of (m+1)/2 on the approximation ratio for truthful-in-expectation mechanisms, determining the optimal ratio as m/2 plus a constant. It also raises the leading constant of the lower bound for universally truthful mechanisms from 3/2−√2 to 1/2, which together with a known upper bound settles that ratio up to lower-order terms. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove a (m+1)/2 lower bound for randomized truthful makespan scheduling, improving the leading constant from about 0.0858 to 1/2.

entry.title: Random matrix analysis of symmetric tensor unfolding, a method for recovering hidden signals from noisy high-order data
entry.summary: A Random Matrix Analysis of Symmetric Tensor Unfolding arXiv · Nov 4, 2026This paper studies recovering a hidden unit vector from a spiked tensor corrupted by symmetric Gaussian noise. Instead of replacing the noise with an i.i.d. tensor as earlier work did, the authors analyze the symmetric model directly using random matrix theory. They show that square unfolding undergoes a sharp phase transition at signal strength around n^((p-2)/4), and derive precise expressions for the spectral distribution, threshold, and overlap. ★★★★ Notable: The authors analyze symmetric tensor unfolding directly via random matrix theory, showing a sharp phase transition at λ≍n^{(p-2)/4} and validating an open conjecture.

entry.title: Information Loss Is All You Need: Post-Quantum TC⁰ Pseudorandomness from Worst-Case Lattices
entry.summary: Information Loss Is All You Need: TC⁰ Pseudorandomness from Worst-Case Lattices arXiv · Nov 4, 2026The paper introduces learning with algebraic rounding (LAR), which applies deterministic integer rounding to blocks of secret-dependent linear measurements and encodes the result in a lattice quotient. For a fixed family with polynomially bounded modulus and dimensions, the authors show these deterministic labels on uniform, secret-independent public matrices are computationally indistinguishable from uniform labels given any polynomial number of classical random examples. Security rests on quantum worst-case hardness of GapSVP and SIVP over general lattices at approximation factor Õ(q). The construction yields a post-quantum weak pseudorandom function with joint key-and-input evaluation in TC⁰, and the paper also proves hardness of learning polynomial-size two-hidden-layer ReLU networks from noiseless uniform random examples. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose learning with algebraic rounding, a deterministic-rounding construction giving a TC0 weak PRF from worst-case lattice hardness, plus ReLU network learning hardness.

entry.title: Tight limits for fair-in-expectation job scheduling on machines
entry.summary: Sharp Bounds for Truthful-in-Expectation Scheduling arXiv · Nov 4, 2026The paper studies randomized mechanisms that schedule indivisible jobs on n unrelated machines, where each selfish machine owner privately knows its job processing times. The mechanisms are truthful in expectation and aim to minimize the expected makespan. For n of at least 7, the authors prove the optimal approximation ratio is (n+1)/2, and they give a matching mechanism. For two machines the optimal ratio is about 1.505995705434, and for three machines it is 2. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a matching lower and upper bound of (n+1)/2 for n≥7 and exact constants for two and three machines, for truthful-in-expectation scheduling.

entry.title: PAC learning where each example has several correct answers
entry.summary: PAC Learning with Multiple Correct Answers arXiv · Nov 4, 2026This paper studies PAC learning when each example has at most ℓ correct labels, and a prediction counts as correct if it lies in that set. Training may reveal the full set, only whether a proposed label is correct, or a single correct label chosen by a demonstrator. The authors show that learning from demonstrations can be much harder than learning from full sets or bandit feedback, and they give dimension-based characterizations of learnability for finite and countable label spaces. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors characterize learnability from full sets, bandit feedback and demonstrations, and report a tight ε^{-ℓ} sample bound with proofs for finite and countable label spaces.

entry.title: Quantum query lower bounds via classical moment matching
entry.summary: Quantum Query Lower Bounds from Classical Moment Matching arXiv · Nov 4, 2026The paper develops a quantum version of the classical moment matching method, which is used to prove lower bounds in property testing. It presents two incomparable quantum moment matching theorems, with lower bounds of Ω(N^{1/2-1/(2r)}) and Ω(N^{1/2-1/(2(2^r-1))}), the latter holding for smaller parameter ranges. The proofs combine a new continuous hybrid argument with the polynomial method. The theorems are applied to obtain optimal lower bounds for k-distinctness, k-star-freeness, planarity and outerplanarity testing. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a quantum moment matching method combining continuous hybrid argument and polynomial method, yielding improved quantum query lower bounds for several property testing problems.

entry.title: Learning intersections of degree-2 polynomial threshold functions beyond multi-index models
entry.summary: Beyond Multi-Index Models: Learning Intersections of Degree-2 PTFs arXiv · Nov 4, 2026The paper presents a PAC learning algorithm for intersections of k degree-2 polynomial threshold functions over R^d under a Gaussian distribution. It achieves error ε in time and samples d^{O(k)}·2^{O_k(log^3(1/ε))}, improving on the d^{O(k^2/ε^2)} running time of polynomial regression. An SQ lower bound shows the d^{Ω(k)} dimension dependence is unavoidable. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a learner whose dimension exponent is independent of accuracy, with a matching SQ lower bound for degree-2 PTF intersections.

entry.title: Constant-factor fair-share guarantees for subadditive valuations
entry.summary: Toward Constant-Factor Maximin Share Guarantees for Subadditive Valuations arXiv · Nov 4, 2026The paper studies maximin share (MMS), a fairness measure for dividing indivisible goods among n agents. For general subadditive valuations, it improves the known guarantee from Ω(1/log log n) to Ω(1/log* n). It also introduces q-partitioning valuations, an intermediate class between subadditive and XOS, and proves constant guarantees when q/n has a positive lower bound. For XOS valuations, the universal guarantee rises from about 0.2353 to 0.3125. ★★★★ Notable: The authors improve the general subadditive MMS guarantee exponentially to Ω(1/log* n) and report constant guarantees for intermediate q-partitioning valuation classes.

entry.title: Interactive Privacy Boosts Accuracy in Edge-Private Subgraph Counting
entry.summary: The Power of Interaction in Locally Edge-Private Subgraph Counting arXiv · Nov 4, 2026This paper studies counting subgraphs of a fixed pattern in any undirected graph under interactive local edge differential privacy. The authors propose a two-round algorithm, Linear Noise Cancellation, with error O(n^{k-3/2}/ε^ℓ) on every graph, showing that one extra interaction round can polynomially improve worst-case accuracy over noninteractive methods. They also give a Predict and Correct framework for graphs with bounded maximum degree and prove matching lower bounds in n and d. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a two-round interactive method improving triangle counting error by √n, with matching lower bounds showing tight bounds.

entry.title: ToolSpace: Tool-centric environment synthesis for training long-horizon AI agents
entry.summary: ToolSpace: Scaling Tool-Centric Environment Synthesis for Long-Horizon Agents arXiv · Nov 4, 2026ToolSpace proposes a framework that builds training environments around tools rather than data, mining dependencies between adjacent tool calls from real MCP service execution traces using deterministic rules. It clusters the resulting tool-composition graph into environments and generates tasks via state-aware random walks, keeping only those that replay successfully. On seven long-horizon tool-use benchmarks, the method substantially raises the average scores of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and GLM-5.2. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose tool-centric environment synthesis mined from execution traces, reporting gains across seven long-horizon tool-use benchmarks.

entry.title: Unified Theory of Capability Degradation in LLM Fine-Tuning via Feature Interference
entry.summary: Unifying and Beyond the Theory of Pervasive Capability Degradation in LLM Post-training SFT from Feature Interference arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies Pervasive Capability Degradation (PCD), where supervised fine-tuning of a large language model on a target task erodes general capabilities learned during pre-training. The authors propose a geometric theory attributing PCD to feature interference under superposition, which unifies existing mitigation methods into six paradigms. They also show that cross-entropy with one-hot supervision cannot resolve PCD alone and introduce the AEGIS loss, which constrains activation margin drift across competing tokens. Tested on 14 SFT tasks across 3 model families, AEGIS reportedly performs well on both target and general capabilities at about 1.3 times the cost of standard SFT. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a feature-interference geometric theory unifying six paradigms and a new AEGIS loss, reporting gains over representative methods across 3 model families and 14 tasks.

entry.title: Computational Complexity of Continuous Contract Design over Polymatroids
entry.summary: The Complexity of Continuous Contract Design over Polymatroids arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies optimal contracts where an agent allocates continuous effort under polymatroid capacity constraints. Linear costs admit polynomial-time computation of an optimal contract, while for quadratic costs the agent's best response is computable but optimizing the principal's share is NP-hard. The authors show an optimal quadratic-cost contract always exists with a share at most 1/2, which yields approximation schemes. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show NP-hardness and exponentially many breakpoints for quadratic-cost contracts over polymatroids, and prove a share of at most 1/2 suffices for approximation.

entry.title: Distributed graph computation that survives node crashes
entry.summary: Local Distributed Computation under Crash Failures arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies deterministic algorithms for locally checkable graph problems in the synchronous LOCAL model, where crashing nodes may send messages to only some neighbors. The authors introduce consistent neighborhoods, which let a fault-free T-round algorithm be simulated locally and remain correct on subgraphs. The paper gives upper and lower bounds on the number of rounds needed to build these views, and reports complexity results for LCL problems and sinkless orientation under crashes. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce consistent neighborhoods for crash-tolerant LOCAL simulation, reporting near-tight upper and lower bounds plus LCL complexity separations.

entry.title: Randomized fair allocation of chores with a few disposals, guaranteeing a near-maximin-share standard
entry.summary: Best-of-Many-Worlds MMS Allocation for Chores with Sublinear Disposals arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies randomized (lottery-based) allocations of indivisible chores under additive costs. It introduces MMS1, a fairness notion requiring each agent's bundle to meet the maximin share bound after removing at most one chore. The main result shows that every instance admits an ex-ante proportional lottery whose every allocation is MMS1, with all but o(n) agents satisfying MMS. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce MMS1 and report ex-ante proportional lotteries where nearly all agents get MMS, improving known chore-allocation fairness bounds.

entry.title: Leakage-resilient computation through matrix refreshing: a way to protect secrets from side-channel leaks
entry.summary: Leakage-Resilient Computation via Matrix Refreshing arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper studies cryptographic methods that keep secrets safe even when side-channel attacks reveal partial information about a device's internal state. A secret is split into two shares held by separate parties, and each refresh multiplies one share by an invertible matrix and the other by its inverse. The authors prove this refresh remains secure under continual local leakage and give explicit bounds on statistical distance. They also present a circuit compiler supporting repeated stateful computation, along with efficient simulation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show matrix refreshing of inner-product shares resists continual local leakage, with bounds for refreshes, a circuit compiler, and simulation.

entry.title: Complexity bounds for nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax optimization with exact proximal access
entry.summary: On the Complexity of Finite-Sum Nonconvex-Strongly-Concave Minimax Optimization with Exact Proximal Oracles arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper studies finite-sum nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax problems, which arise in adversarial training and distributionally robust learning. It shows that neither unrestricted adaptive algorithms nor exact component proximal steps improve the polynomial complexity. The authors give a lower bound on the number of component queries needed to find an epsilon-stationary point, and note that a gradient-only method matches this rate up to a logarithmic factor. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show exact proximal oracles and unrestricted adaptivity fail to improve polynomial complexity, giving a lower bound matched by a gradient method up to a log factor.

entry.title: Reducing Logprob Without Causal Verification: Checking Whether SAE-Based Methods Really Suppress Personal Data in LLMs
entry.summary: Reducing Logprob Without Causal Verification: Diagnosing SAE-Based PII Suppression in LLMs arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper examines methods that use sparse autoencoder (SAE) feature interventions to stop large language models from leaking personally identifiable information, which are usually judged by how much they lower log-probability. The authors show this measure cannot tell targeted suppression apart from side effects of large activation changes. Across 36 model, layer, and PII-type cases, 17 looked successful on log-probability alone, but only 1 passed their multi-metric framework. The authors propose causally grounded suppression based on circuit-level localization and causal mediation analysis as a new research direction. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show logprob reduction cannot separate feature-specific suppression from magnitude artifacts, testing 36 cases against random-direction controls with multiple metrics.

entry.title: Logarithmic comparison queries for fair item allocation
entry.summary: Logarithmic Comparison-Query Complexity for EF1 Allocations arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper studies how many comparison queries are needed to find an allocation of indivisible items among n agents that is envy-free up to one item (EF1). Algorithms may only ask which of two bundles an agent prefers, never seeing numerical values. The authors give algorithms using O(log m) queries for every fixed n≥2, matching a known Ω(log m) lower bound. The results cover both chores with nonnegative costs and goods with nonnegative valuations. ★★★★ Notable: The authors resolve an open question, giving O(log m) comparison-query EF1 algorithms for every fixed n≥2, matching the known lower bound.

entry.title: What removing a graph edge means: intervention-aware fidelity for GNN explanations
entry.summary: What Does It Mean to Remove an Edge? Intervention-Aware Fidelity for Graph Neural Network Explanations arXiv · Nov 3, 2026Graph neural network explanations are often judged by deleting their top-ranked edges and measuring how the model output changes. The paper argues that deleting an edge in message passing can mean two different interventions: structural deletion, which recomputes graph-dependent quantities, and message suppression, which keeps the structure but blocks the edge's message. The authors give conditions under which the two are equivalent and test them on nine datasets with GIN, GCN, and GATv2 models. They find that the relative fidelity of edge rankings often depends on which intervention is used for evaluation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors separate structural deletion from message suppression, derive exact equivalence conditions, and report that relative fidelity of edge rankings shifts with the evaluation intervention acros

entry.title: A paper showing self-stabilising approximate clock synchronisation needs linear time
entry.summary: Self-stabilising approximate clock synchronisation requires linear time arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies clock synchronisation in distributed systems where processes may start in arbitrary states and up to f processes may suffer non-transient faults. The authors prove that deterministic self-stabilising approximate clock synchronisation tasks require Ω(f) time to stabilise, giving the first non-trivial time lower bound for these tasks. The result shows that tolerating both transient and non-transient faults is costly even for approximate synchronisation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove the first nontrivial Ω(f) time lower bound for self-stabilising approximate clock synchronisation, using a topological argument.

entry.title: BrainwashedLLM: Jailbreaking Large Reasoning Models by Automatically Discovering Adversarial Chains of Thought
entry.summary: BrainwashedLLM: Jailbreaking via Automated Adversarial Chain of Thoughts Discovery arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper examines the safety risks of the explicit chain-of-thought reasoning produced by Large Reasoning Models, showing that the reasoning trace itself can serve as an attack vector. The authors propose BrainwashedLLM, which uses reinforcement learning (GRPO) to train a small white-box model to generate adversarial reasoning traces, then injects these traces as prefixes into larger black-box reasoning models. The method reportedly achieves ASR@5 between 0.74 and 0.98 across four state-of-the-art models without querying the target during attack construction. The authors argue that exposed chain-of-thought is a vulnerability and suggest architectural defenses such as isolating the reasoning buffer. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use RL to optimize a small model's reasoning traces as an attack surface, transferring them zero-shot; the abstract reports ASR@5 across four large reasoning models.

entry.title: Proving the Wrong Program: Compiler Bugs as a Threat to zkVM Guarantees
entry.summary: Proving the Wrong Program: Miscompilations as a Threat to zkVM Guarantees arXiv · Nov 3, 2026A zero-knowledge virtual machine (zkVM) lets an untrusted prover convince a verifier that a program, usually Rust compiled to RISC-V, ran correctly. This paper presents the first empirical study of miscompilation as a threat to the SP1 and Jolt zkVMs, assembling 88 known rustc and LLVM bugs with Rust reproducers. Of these, 48 cause SP1 guests and 46 cause Jolt guests to commit wrong outputs. Existing guest programs are rarely affected by accident, but an attacker can deliberately trigger these bugs by contributing crafted code. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors report the first empirical study of miscompilations threatening zkVM guarantees, reproducing 88 known bugs on SP1 and Jolt and showing LLM-crafted triggering patches.

entry.title: Lower bounds for adaptive relaxed locally decodable codes
entry.summary: Lower Bounds for Adaptive Relaxed Locally Decodable Codes via the Capped Horvitz--Thompson Estimator arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper proves a nearly optimal lower bound on the blocklength of general relaxed locally decodable codes (RLDCs), extending prior results to nonlinear encodings and adaptive decoders with two-sided error. It shows that any q-query RLDC must have blocklength n = k^{1+Ω(1/q)}, closely matching a known upper bound. The proof reduces the problem to estimating the output distribution of adaptive decoders, using a capped Horvitz–Thompson estimator with bounded discrete derivatives on the p-biased cube. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors extend RLDC lower bounds to nonlinear encodings and adaptive two-sided-error decoders, obtaining a nearly tight n=k^{1+Ω(1/q)} bound via a capped Horvitz–Thompson estimator.

entry.title: Does LinUCB Need Valid Confidence Sets?
entry.summary: Does LinUCB Need Valid Confidence Sets? arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper shows that replacing LinUCB's usual confidence width with any fixed positive constant still yields sublinear regret when the action set is M-smooth and m-strongly convex. It gives a high-probability regret bound for this generalised method, α-LinUCB, indicating that valid confidence sets are not required for LinUCB to succeed. The analysis uses a logarithmically capped spectral potential, and at the standard width it gives an O((M/m)d√(T log T)) regret bound, improving the horizon dependence of classical LinUCB by a factor of √log T. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show fixed-width α-LinUCB keeps sublinear regret on smooth strongly convex action sets, introducing a log-capped spectral potential improving the classical bound by √log T.

entry.title: Distributed LTL Synthesis under Arbitrary Message Adversaries
entry.summary: Distributed LTL Synthesis under Arbitrary Message Adversaries arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies how two processes communicating in rounds over unreliable links can be automatically given distributed programs that satisfy linear temporal logic specifications, even though at least one message is delivered each round. It shows that this synthesis is undecidable in general, even when messages carry complete causal histories. The authors characterize exactly which communication restrictions, modeled as message adversaries, make synthesis decidable. For omega-regular adversaries, synthesis is decidable if and only if the image of the adversary's histories in the unit interval is nowhere dense. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a complete characterization of decidable distributed LTL synthesis under message adversaries, linking it topologically to repeated bounded-time consensus.

entry.title: A Benchmark and Model for Judging 3D Gaussian Splatting Video Quality Across Geometry and Color
entry.summary: 3DGS-VBench+ and 3DGSV-Assessor: A Multi-Dimensional Subjective Benchmark and a Reference-Flexible Objective Model for 3D Gaussian Splatting Video Quality Assessment arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper addresses how to assess the quality of videos rendered from 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models, which are compressed and can suffer distortions in geometry and color. The authors introduce 3DGS-VBench+, a subjective benchmark of 3,036 reconstructions with 9,108 human quality scores covering overall, geometry, and color quality. They also propose 3DGSV-Assessor, a multimodal model that scores all three dimensions in one pass and supports both reduced-reference and no-reference assessment. The model reportedly correlates strongly with human judgments and generalizes zero-shot to other novel view synthesis benchmarks.</summary> ★★★★ Notable: The authors present a multi-dimensional 3DGS video quality benchmark and a reference-flexible model, reporting 9,108 MOS annotations, state-of-the-art correlation, zero-shot generalization, and public

entry.title: Computational Difficulty of Exact Autobidding Equilibria
entry.summary: On the Complexity of Exact Autobidding Equilibria arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies how hard it is to compute autobidding equilibria, which link advertisers' value multipliers or participation probabilities through aggregate budget and ROI constraints. It establishes the exact computational complexity of finding these equilibria in several canonical settings, including second-price ROI pacing and budget- or ROI-constrained generalized second-price sponsored shopping. It also analyzes the complexity of approximating the equilibrium control vector when the target accuracy is given as input. ★★★★ Notable: The authors establish FIXP-completeness of exact autobidding equilibrium computation across several canonical settings, a new complexity characterization relevant to computational economics.

entry.title: EvoCG: A self-evolving precision-control method that speeds up conjugate gradient solvers
entry.summary: EvoCG: Self-Evolving Precision Control for Faster Conjugate Gradient arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper presents EvoCG, a mixed-precision conjugate gradient solver that uses a reinforcement-learning policy to choose precision for each tile during iteration. It is supported by a Tile-CSC mixed-precision SpMV kernel and a low-overhead in-loop runtime. Tested on 47 SPD matrices, it reports geometric-mean speedups over several baseline solvers and a time-to-solution gain over an FP64 version at the cost of more iterations. ★★★★ Notable: The authors treat tile-wise precision as online RL control within CG iterations, co-designed with a mixed-precision SpMV; reported 1.9–7x geometric-mean speedups across 47 SPD matrices.

entry.title: Formalizing PTX in Lean to Prove GPU Kernel Correctness
entry.summary: Formalizing PTX in Lean to Prove GPU Kernel Correctness arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper presents a method for mathematically formalizing PTX, NVIDIA's GPU intermediate assembly language, to model and reason about common deep learning GPU kernel patterns. These include acquire-release, tensor cores, proxies, async operations, multi-kernel pipelines, and data-dependent control flow. The authors implement the approach in Lean and use it to prove the correctness of simple implementations of a WGMMA GEMM kernel, FlashAttention, and a 3-kernel MoE pipeline. ★★★★ Notable: The authors formalize PTX in Lean, covering tensor cores and async operations, and prove correctness of WGMMA GEMM, FlashAttention, and a MoE pipeline.

entry.title: Binary Huffman coding with unequal letter costs is NP-complete
entry.summary: Binary Huffman Coding with Unequal Letter Costs Is NP-Complete arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies optimal binary prefix coding when letters have unequal costs. The authors prove that deciding whether a binary prefix-free code with frequency-weighted cost at most a given threshold exists is NP-complete, even when the letter costs are consecutive positive integers (M, M+1) given as input. The proof uses two polynomial-time reductions starting from Planar Independent Set. The result implies that finding an optimal code is NP-hard. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors prove NP-completeness of binary Huffman coding with unequal letter costs, via two polynomial-time reductions from Planar Independent Set.

entry.title: Entropy-gated adaptive correction for object hallucination in vision-language models
entry.summary: Entropy-Gated Dynamic Rectification for Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models arXiv · Nov 3, 2026Large vision-language models sometimes name objects that are not in the image. The paper proposes EGDR, which adjusts an existing latent steering gate's threshold using the entropy of the previous step's logits: high entropy lowers the threshold, while low entropy keeps the calibrated setting. On LLaVA-1.5-7B, it further reduces CHAIR hallucination scores compared with the static gate. It needs no extra forward pass and adds roughly 2% latency. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use predictive entropy as a causally available signal to dynamically set the steering threshold, reporting CHAIR gains on LLaVA-1.5-7B and LLaVA-NeXT-7B with public code.

entry.title: Sketchpad: a small vision-language model with certified exact arithmetic
entry.summary: Sketchpad: certified exact arithmetic with a small vision-language model arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper presents Sketchpad, in which a small vision-language model (Qwen3.5-0.8B with a low-rank adapter) performs arithmetic step by step on a rendered sheet, reading only a three-cell view per step. The authors prove in Lean that exactness on all input lengths reduces to checking a finite set of views. They report that the model solved all 200 pre-registered problems in a web browser and all 220 sums and products tested, outperforming a comparison model on that set. ★★★★ Notable: The authors reduce exact arithmetic to a finite checkable property, prove it in Lean, and report verification on 2,446 views and several problem sets.

entry.title: Hidden evaluation-tool errors can reorder AI agent leaderboard rankings
entry.summary: Silent Instrument Errors Reorder Agent Leaderboards arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper argues that scores on public agent leaderboards can be distorted by flaws in the evaluation infrastructure, such as grading, cost logging, action recording, and evaluator versioning, without any visible sign. Using two public leaderboards, the authors show cases where re-grading saved results without rerunning agents changes the ordering. They propose checks including reporting the graded fraction, aggregating cost from root spans, tagging the provenance of recorded actions, and pinning evaluator versions. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors audit two public agent leaderboards and report three instrument errors that silently reorder rankings, arguing evaluation infrastructure is part of the measurement.

entry.title: Voluntary Servitude: Weaponized Safety Warnings Used to Steer AI Agents
entry.summary: Voluntary Servitude: Weaponized Safety Warning Mechanisms for Controlling AI Agents arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper shows that attackers can manipulate LLM agents by exploiting their own harm-avoidance behavior. A single fabricated hazard, written as an ordinary review, causes the agent to rule out legitimate options and choose the attacker's target, without any injected command. Tests across six models and ten consumer-service domains found this steers agents about as often as instruction injection while evading injection detectors. Adding a corroboration requirement to the agent's instructions removes roughly 95% of exposure against a non-adaptive attacker without retraining. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose steering agents via their own harm avoidance, report tests across six models and ten domains, and evaluate a mitigation.

entry.title: Do Conversation Skills Carry From Text to Speech? A Multilingual Benchmark
entry.summary: Do Multi-Turn Conversational Capabilities Carry Over from Text to Speech? A Parallel Multilingual Benchmark arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper introduces Omnilingua-AudioMC, a strictly parallel multilingual extension of Audio MultiChallenge with 354 conversations and 1,404 rubric items across ten languages. It compares six speech-language models on the same conversations given as reference transcripts versus direct speech input. Results show transcript performance is an unreliable proxy for multilingual spoken conversational ability, and that the representation of preceding spoken context is a key source of recoverable degradation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors build a strictly parallel ten-language benchmark comparing transcript and speech conditions, reporting experiments on six speech-language models and paired rubric analysis.

entry.title: Computational Hardness of Approximate Quantum Circuit Membership and Optimization
entry.summary: On the Hardness of Approximate Quantum Circuit Membership and Optimization arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper studies approximate membership for quantum circuits: deciding whether a given circuit lies within a distance of a fixed set of unitaries. It extends earlier results for the identity set under promise assumptions to promise-free inputs, other unitary sets such as Clifford or generalized permutation matrices, and several distance metrics. The authors show that the problem is PP-hard across wide ranges of parameters, with hardness persisting across quantum resources and metrics, which implies PP-hardness of certain circuit optimization tasks. ★★★★ Notable: The authors generalize known QMA-completeness of approximate identity to promise-free inputs and several unitary sets and metrics, reporting PP-hardness with implications for circuit optimization.

entry.title: Proper agnostic learning of affine halfspaces under log-concave distributions
entry.summary: Proper Agnostic Learning of Affine Halfspaces under Log-Concave Marginals arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper presents a proper constant-factor agnostic learner for affine halfspaces under full-dimensional log-concave marginals. It uses independent labeled samples for arbitrary binary labels and returns one affine halfspace with error at most C·OPT+ε. Sample and arithmetic complexity are polynomial in dimension, inverse accuracy, and the log of the inverse failure probability. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a proper constant-factor agnostic learner for affine halfspaces under log-concave marginals, with a global-versus-balanced disagreement comparison as the core geometric result and pol

entry.title: Gaussian difference dynamics: classical randomized algorithms that beat the 2^{n/2} barrier for lattice sampling and shortest vectors
entry.summary: Gaussian Difference Dynamics: Breaking the 2ⁿ/2 Barrier for the Shortest Vector Problem and Discrete Gaussian Sampling arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper presents classical randomized algorithms that break the 2^{n/2} time barrier for discrete Gaussian sampling and the Shortest Vector Problem on lattices. It introduces Gaussian difference dynamics, a framework that tracks expected vector counts and pairwise clustering through repeated differencing. The authors also address batch sampling and answer a question of Stephens-Davidowitz about centered sampling. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce Gaussian difference dynamics and report discrete Gaussian sampling in (3/2)^{n/2} time on arbitrary lattices, breaking the 2^{n/2} barrier.

entry.title: How task order affects continual learning: an empirical study and order-aware evaluation for motion forecasting
entry.summary: What Is the Influence of Task Order in Continual Learning? An Empirical Study and Order-Aware Evaluation for Motion Forecasting arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper examines how the order of tasks affects continual learning, using four road-layout tasks from the INTERACTION dataset for motion forecasting. It covers all 24 task orders, four algorithms, and three training replicates. Task order accounts for 65% to 91% of the variation in current-task error and backward transfer, and most of this effect comes from which task is learned first. The authors recommend that benchmarks declare their order distribution and report order-resolved and starting-task-resolved results alongside aggregate scores. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose order-aware evaluation of continual learning, reporting 288 runs showing starting task identity dominates order effects in motion forecasting.

entry.title: Can harmless skills make LLM agents behave unsafely?
entry.summary: Can Benign Skills Induce Misaligned Behavior in LLM Agents? arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies whether adding reusable benign skills to LLM agents can lead them to take external actions that violate safety requirements. Comparing agents with and without skills across five LLM backbones and three benchmarks, the authors find that skills raise benign task accuracy by 10.3 percentage points on average but also raise the unsafe action rate by 10.3 points. The paper also examines factors that worsen this risk and shows that a guard checking tool actions before execution reduces violations while keeping gains on benign tasks. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors identify skill-induced misalignment, comparing agents with and without benign skills across five backbones and three benchmarks, and test a pre-execution guard.

entry.title: How Much Risk Does a Data-Driven Policy Carry?
entry.summary: How Risky Is Your Data-Driven Policy? arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper measures the risk of data-driven policies using the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) of losses over the training sample, policy randomization, and future outcomes. Regret relative to an oracle that knows the distribution splits into post-sample regret and a sample-risk premium. It gives conditions under which the premium vanishes and how large it is relative to post-sample regret, along with convergence rates for sample average approximation in two settings. In finite-sample numerical examples, the premium accounts for roughly 74% to 97% of regret. ★★★★ Notable: The authors decompose data-driven policy regret into post-sample regret and a sample-risk premium, characterize its vanishing conditions, and report numerical SAA examples.

entry.title: "The Native Menace": Host-to-Browser Cross-Boundary Attacks via Native Messaging
