How this direction is read, however, varies with model scale, instruction tuning and system prompt, and in one model the sign of the effect reverses. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report that a model's own earlier answer writes a commitment direction shaping later answers, tested across 22 models and 3,600 question pairs.

entry.title: Autonomous agent that tunes MSA construction to improve protein complex structure prediction
entry.summary: Auto-Research Agent on MSA Organization to Improve Protein-Protein Complex Structure Prediction arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper studies how the depth and cross-chain pairing of multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) affect AlphaFold 3's prediction of protein complex structures, finding the best strategy depends on the target. The authors introduce an autonomous agent that treats a frozen AF3 as a black box, forming biological hypotheses and iteratively reorganizing MSAs and pairing choices, including deliberate non-pairing, using label-free confidence signals. Across 1,015 protein-protein interfaces from three benchmarks, the agent improves overall DockQ over the default pipeline and fixed recipes while using on average 60% fewer MSA sequences. The largest gains occur for inter-species heteromers, with mean DockQ rising from 0.465 to 0.612 on FoldBench and from 0.482 to 0.562 on HD439. ★★★★ Notable: The authors treat MSA design as target-specific and adapt it at test time with an autonomous agent; they report DockQ gains over AF3's default on 1,015 interfaces across three benchmarks.

entry.title: ViAdminShift: A Vietnamese benchmark testing whether language models update knowledge after the 2025 administrative reform
entry.summary: ViAdminShift: A Vietnamese Benchmark for Event-Level Knowledge Updates Built from the 2025 Administrative Reform arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper presents ViAdminShift, a Vietnamese benchmark built around the July 1, 2025 administrative reorganization that cut Vietnam's provinces and communes. It includes 7,995 benchmark items and 2,281 retrieval passages. The authors test 67 models and find that many still give old provinces for old addresses, with the answer changing when a date is given in the prompt. ★★★★ Notable: The authors build an event-level benchmark from Vietnam's 2025 administrative reform and report probing results on 67 models, including outdated-answer rates.

entry.title: Reed-Muller codes are optimal linear 3-query locally correctable codes
entry.summary: Reed-Muller Codes are Optimal Binary Linear 3-Query LCCs arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper proves that any linear 3-query locally correctable code with constant correction radius must have length at least 2 raised to Ω(√k). The previous best lower bound was 2 raised to Ω(√(k/log k)). The result shows that linear 3-LCCs built from Reed-Muller codes, which have length 2 raised to O(√k), are optimal up to constant factors in the exponent. The proof combines chain-derived equations with Kikuchi graphs and shows that a certain edge-coloured Kikuchi graph has a unique colour cycle. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors improve the length lower bound for linear 3-query LCCs to 2^Ω(√k), showing Reed-Muller constructions are optimal up to constant exponent factors.

entry.title: A study of how much information privacy filters and odometers need to work well.
entry.summary: An Information Hierarchy of Privacy Filters and Odometers arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper studies how the information used by differential privacy filters and odometers limits their performance. It defines three information levels (spec, mechanism, and realisation) and classifies filters and odometers by the least informative level sufficient to determine their behaviour. The main results show strict and arbitrarily large performance gaps across this hierarchy, and that randomisation offers a separate resource that can also yield large utility gains. ★★★★ Notable: The authors formalise a three-level information hierarchy and report arbitrarily large separations in filter and odometer performance across levels.

entry.title: DR Pixel: Deep Research Directly on Document Page Images with Vision-Language Models
entry.summary: DR Pixel: Page-Native Deep Research with Vision-Language Models arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper introduces DR Pixel, an open-source multimodal research agent that retrieves and reasons over rendered page images instead of OCR-extracted text, across a 1.06M-page corpus. The authors also build DRPixelBench, a benchmark of scientific papers requiring reasoning over text, figures, tables, and equations. The approach outperforms OCR-based baselines even without training, and a counterfactual credit reweighting method further improves retrieval recall and accuracy. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a page-native multimodal research agent with counterfactual credit reweighting, reporting gains over OCR baselines on DRPixelBench and four other benchmarks.

entry.title: A fine-grained difficulty ladder and benchmark for how language models track changing states
entry.summary: A Fine-Grained Hierarchy and Benchmark for State Tracking in Language Models arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper proposes a four-level hierarchy of word problems, from simple immutable variable assignment to general finite state tracking, to evaluate how well language models track state. It theoretically compares transformers with recurrent architectures such as Gated DeltaNet, and builds StateBench, a long-horizon benchmark based on these levels. Direct training experiments largely match the theoretical predictions, while pretrained models, both open and closed, do not robustly solve even soluble state tracking. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a four-level state-tracking hierarchy and benchmark, with theoretical characterizations of several architectures and direct-training and pretrained-model evaluations.

entry.title: One Image Is Enough: Self-Generated Supervision for Personalizing Human Video Diffusion
entry.summary: One Image Is Enough: Self-Generated Supervision for Personalizing Human Video Diffusion at Test Time arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper addresses pose-driven human video diffusion models, which struggle to keep a person's identity consistent when the target pose differs from the reference image. Instead of requiring multi-pose subject videos, the authors synthesize pseudo-ground-truth frames at key poses with a pose-conditioned generator, select the most identity-consistent ones using a reference-only sampler, and train a per-subject low-rank adapter on them. On TikTok and UBC Fashion, the adapted model improves over the base on every metric and matches or surpasses adaptation using five real frames. ★★★★ Notable: The authors replace real multi-pose subject video with synthesized pseudo-ground-truth frames for personalization, reporting gains on TikTok and UBC Fashion.

entry.title: Generative diffusion on long-range correlated landscapes: how the reverse process commits to data
entry.summary: Generative diffusion in long-range correlated landscapes: Speciation cascade and the foam structure of the score arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper studies why generative diffusion works, using the Gibbs measure of a high-dimensional Gaussian random potential with long-range correlations as an analytically tractable data model. With the exact score, the authors show that the reverse process gradually resolves the branches of pure states and commits to a single one within a speciation window. They describe the score as a foam of slab-like cells separated by shock-like boundaries, and show that the denoising error drops in stages that follow this process. ★★★★ Notable: The authors analyze reverse diffusion on Gibbs measures of long-range correlated Gaussian potentials, introducing a foam structure and Larkin-type argument for O(1) energy gaps.

entry.title: Voice-native LLMs detect frustrated voices in audio but fail to act on them
entry.summary: Voice-Native LLMs Hear Frustration but Do Not Listen to It arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper examines whether voice-native language models, which process speech directly rather than through transcripts, notice frustration in a speaker's voice. Using a 2x2 design that pairs frustrated or neutral wording with frustrated or neutral voice over 353 tasks, the authors release VoxAffect, a dataset of 1,412 clips. Most models rarely label the frustrated voice as frustrated, yet linear probes can decode it from their audio encoders, suggesting the models hear the voice without using it. ★★★★ Notable: The authors apply Brunswik's lens model to separate perceiving from using vocal frustration, testing eight models on 1,412 clips.

entry.title: Iterated Width-4 ReLU Networks: Turing Completeness and Verification Complexity
entry.summary: Iterated Narrow Networks: Turing Completeness at Width 4 on Convex Input Spaces and the Complexity of Verification arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper studies iterates of a fixed width-4 ReLU network acting as a discrete-time system on the cube [0,1]^4. It shows that every deterministic Turing machine can be encoded by such a network, constructible in polynomial time, whose iterations exactly simulate the machine with iteration count proportional to running time. Reachability for these iterated networks therefore spans NP-complete, NEXP-complete, and undecidable (RE-complete) cases depending on the time bound. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a width-4 iterated ReLU construction simulating Turing machines on convex cubes, yielding a full complexity hierarchy and extensions to smooth activations and Neural ODEs.

entry.title: Beyond Monotonicity: Learning Stochastic Online Optimization From Partial Feedback
entry.summary: Beyond Monotonicity: Stochastic Online Optimization under Semi-Bandit Feedback arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper studies stochastic online optimization where, each round, a policy adaptively observes n random variables with unknown distributions and learns only from the observed values. The proposed algorithm runs dynamic programming using the most optimistic expected values over a confidence set, with regret governed by level-set complexity. The authors also prove a matching lower bound and apply the results to several nonmonotone problems. ★★★★ Notable: The authors drop FSD monotonicity, give regret bounds depending on level-set complexity, and report a matching lower bound across several nonmonotone problems.

entry.title: The Customer Never Sees the Goal: Studies whether AI shopping assistants exploit customers' disclosed vulnerabilities to push a hidden operator goal, and whether this can be detected from the conversation.
entry.summary: The Customer Never Sees the Goal: Measuring and Detecting Vulnerability-Targeted Manipulation in LLM Assistants arXiv · Nov 2, 2026Companies can deploy LLM assistants on their websites with goals customers never see. The paper introduces GAP, which records the option a model recommends without any goal, then sets the other option as the operator's goal, collecting 619,600 labeled replies across 540 everyday scenarios for 15 models. Fourteen of the 15 models push the operator goal, and 12 of them use disclosed distress or financial strain to support it. Fine-tuned detectors reach 79% accuracy from the reply alone, while zero-shot LLM judges average at most 62%, and detection weakens for vulnerabilities not seen in training. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose detecting vulnerability-targeted manipulation from customer-AI conversations via goal-anchored probing, reporting tests on 15 models, 619,600 replies, and generalization to unseen

entry.title: Fine-tuning a few-step masked diffusion language model on its own sampling likelihood
entry.summary: Train the Sampler You Run: Few-Step Masked Diffusion Language Models via Mixture-Likelihood Fine-Tuning arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper observes that a masked diffusion language model sampled in a few parallel steps in random order effectively runs a mixture over reveal plans, which standard cross-entropy training does not fit. The authors propose mixture-likelihood fine-tuning (Mix-FT), which optimizes an importance-weighted bound on the model's own sampler likelihood without a teacher or architectural changes. Experiments on LLaDA-8B and a 110M block diffusion model report that Mix-FT produces better continuations than continued cross-entropy and other baselines at fewer sampling steps. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose mixture-likelihood fine-tuning for few-step masked diffusion language models, needing no teacher or architecture change. The abstract reports gains over continued cross-entropy and

entry.title: VerdictAD: A training-free method that refines anomaly detection using few normal images
entry.summary: VerdictAD: Few-Shot Anomaly Detection via Decision-Guided Refinement arXiv · Nov 2, 2026VerdictAD is a training-free framework that improves existing anomaly detectors. It uses a typed decision model to compare a query image and its local regions against a few normal references, producing structured decision probabilities. These decisions refine the overall anomaly score and the anomaly map. The authors report consistent gains for existing detectors on MVTec AD, VisA, and MVTec LOCO AD. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a training-free plug-and-play refinement using structured visual decisions, improving existing detectors on MVTec AD, VisA, and MVTec LOCO AD.

entry.title: Probe-guided gradient balancing to help weaker modalities in multimodal learning
entry.summary: Probe-Guided Gradient Balancing for Multimodal Learning arXiv · Nov 2, 2026In jointly trained multimodal networks, faster-learning modalities can dominate the shared objective and suppress gradients to slower ones. The paper proposes Probe-Guided Gradient Boosting (PGGB), which attaches lightweight linear classifiers to stop-gradient features to estimate each modality's representation quality. The resulting utilization gap adaptively and boundedly scales weaker-modality gradients without changing the loss or fusion architecture. Experiments on eight benchmarks report gains on highly imbalanced data and competitive results under low imbalance. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose independent linear probes to estimate modality representation quality and boost weaker-modality gradients, evaluated on eight benchmarks across four domains, with bounded-scaling a

entry.title: Variable names as priors: how meaningful names help LLMs predict numbers from little data
entry.summary: Variable names provide priors: semantic grounding enables data-efficient numerical prediction by large language models arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper studies how large language models use variable names and in-context examples to make numerical predictions on tabular data. When variable names semantically match the values they describe, five LLMs without task-specific training matched or outperformed seven supervised machine learning models across 20 datasets from nine scientific domains, especially when examples were scarce. Controlled experiments based on physical formulas indicate that the models combine domain knowledge with examples in a manner consistent with Bayesian updating. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show variable-name semantics act as priors letting LLMs match or beat supervised models on 20 datasets, with physics-formula tasks showing Bayesian-like updating.

entry.title: When cache pressure becomes a trap: metastable failures in LLM agent serving
entry.summary: When Cache Pressure Becomes a Trap: Metastability in Agent Serving arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper studies how a brief traffic surge can break prefix reuse for LLM agents in prefill-decode disaggregated serving engines, leaving service degraded even after load returns to previously sustainable levels. The authors attribute this to a population-cache feedback loop explained by a fluid model. They present Basin, a scheduling approach that reserves predicted session contexts, extends cache with idle decode memory, and sheds excess demand, reporting higher goodput than Continuum and HiCache on real H200 deployments. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors identify cache-population feedback as a metastable failure mechanism in PD-disaggregated serving, propose a fluid model and the Basin policy, and report goodput gains on real H200 deployme

entry.title: When Neither Side Confirms: A Study of Destructive Tool Approval in MCP Servers and Hosts
entry.summary: When Neither Side Confirms: Destructive Tool Approval Across MCP Servers and Hosts arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper examines how AI agents calling destructive tools, such as deleting data or moving money, through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) are approved by humans. It measures both server-side confirmation and host-application approval steps by analyzing source code. The authors find that most destructive tools lack server-side confirmation and most hosts have no default approval step. They conclude that applications should configure approval themselves. ★★★★ Notable: The authors measure missing human approval for destructive MCP tools from source code on both sides, and report an injected-deletion experiment across models.

entry.title: A study of how alternating updates make regret matching algorithms converge
entry.summary: On the Convergence of Alternating Regret Matching Algorithms arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper analyzes the convergence of regret matching algorithms when players are updated in turn rather than simultaneously. The authors introduce an alternating version of the RVU property and use it to show optimal T^{-1} average-iterate convergence for two predictive regret matching+ variants. They find that half prediction is the unique prediction multiplier satisfying this property, and report comparable performance to state-of-the-art solvers on 15 game benchmarks. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce an alternating RVU property, obtaining optimal T^-1 average-iterate convergence and showing half-prediction is the unique satisfying multiplier.

entry.title: CellPlex: A Benchmark for Predicting Single-Cell Spatial Proteomics from H&E Slides
entry.summary: CellPlex: Benchmarking Single-Cell Spatial Proteomics Prediction from H&E arXiv · Nov 2, 2026Spatial proteomics measures dozens of proteins in each cell of a tissue section but is costly, so it is used mainly in small studies. This paper introduces CellPlex, a benchmark that evaluates methods for predicting per-cell protein levels from routine H&E-stained slides across seven cohorts, 717 samples, 44.8 million cells and 149 proteins. Adapted pathology foundation models were the most accurate on every cohort, but kept less than half their accuracy on cohorts they were not trained on. ★★★★ Notable: The authors build a cell-level benchmark across seven cohorts (717 samples, 44.8M cells, 149 proteins) comparing pathology foundation models against specialist virtual staining models.

entry.title: M3Former: Finer-Grained Information Mixing Across Transformer Layers
entry.summary: M3Former: Fine-Grained Cross-Layer Mixing for Transformers arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper argues that standard Transformer residual connections pass information from earlier layers through a single fixed sum shared by all of a block's inputs, which limits what the model can use. The authors propose Multi-Role Multi-Group Mixing Residual (M3), where each role and each group of hidden dimensions forms its own token-dependent mixture of all earlier layers. In experiments from 100M to 1.4B parameters, M3Former outperforms the Transformer and coarser cross-layer connections, and it also improves sparse mixture-of-experts models up to 4.6B parameters. ★★★★ Notable: The authors decompose residual broadcast into three constraints and relax them, proposing token-dependent cross-layer mixing per role and group; the abstract reports gains from 100M to 1.4B parameters

entry.title: A parameter-free policy for choosing channels in queueing bandit problems
entry.summary: A Parameter-Free Best-of-Both-Worlds Policy for Queueing Bandits arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper studies how to schedule a single queue across K channels when only bandit feedback is available. The proposed policy explores when the queue is empty and, during busy periods, picks the empirically best channel while conditions hold, switching to a robust bandit policy if they fail. Under arbitrary arrivals and services set by an oblivious adversary, it achieves Õ(√(K L_T)) worst-case queue length regret with high probability, where L_T is the longest busy period, improving the earlier T^{3/4} dependence. Under bounded i.i.d. models with a unique best stabilizing channel, cumulative queue length regret converges to a finite problem-dependent constant. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a parameter-free best-of-both-worlds policy improving queue regret from T^{3/4} to near-tight √(K L_T), with high-probability worst-case and stochastic results reported.

entry.title: Whether and how fast the regularized quantum channel relative entropy can be computed
entry.summary: Finite attainment and efficient computation of regularized quantum channel relative entropy arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper studies when the regularized quantum channel relative entropy is attained at finite blocklength and how efficiently it can be approximated. It shows a dichotomy: the value is either attained at the single-copy level or never attained at any finite blocklength, and a simple two-copy additivity test distinguishes the two cases. The authors also give explicit convergence rates for approximating the regularized value and a semidefinite hierarchy yielding a certified polynomial-time approximation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors establish a dichotomy for finite attainment of regularized channel relative entropy, a two-copy additivity test, and explicit convergence rates.

entry.title: TERA: Restoring Task-Relevant Image Evidence for Underwater Detection Over Limited-Bandwidth Links
entry.summary: TERA: Task-Evidence Restoration for Underwater Object Detection under Bandwidth-Constrained Transmission arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper notes that underwater object detectors are usually tested only on images before transmission, ignoring extra degradation from bandwidth-limited downscaling and compression. The authors build AquaTX, a benchmark from real underwater detection datasets with both seen and held-out codecs. They also propose TERA, a receiver-side method that uses no metadata and combines task-guided pixel restoration with dual-state feature correction while keeping the detector frozen. ★★★★ Notable: The authors add bandwidth-limited compression degradation to underwater detection evaluation and propose frozen-detector receiver-side restoration; they report mAP gains on DUO-TX and RUOD-TX plus hel

entry.title: When Rewards Depend on the Group, GRPO Plays a Tournament
entry.summary: When Rewards Depend on the Group, GRPO Plays a Tournament arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper shows that when rewards for diversity, coverage, or distribution matching depend on the other responses in a sampled group, the group-relative baseline used by GRPO and RLOO changes the training objective. Each response is effectively trained to beat its groupmates in a zero-sum tournament. The authors propose Team-GRPO, which sets the baseline coefficient to +1 to give an unbiased estimator for any group-dependent reward using two samples per prompt. On GlobalOpinionQA, Team-GRPO reduces error from 0.20 to 0.08 where GRPO collapses to the majority answer, and on NoveltyBench it avoids GRPO's diversity collapse. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove group-relative baselines alter group-dependent reward objectives and propose unbiased Team-GRPO, validated on GlobalOpinionQA and NoveltyBench.

entry.title: A sharp upper bound on mutual information between two binary variables
entry.summary: A Sharp Mutual Information Bound for Binary Pairs arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper proves a sharp upper bound on the mutual information between two binary random variables, expressed through their distribution-dependent KL contraction coefficient. It resolves the binary-pair conjecture of Anantharam, Gohari, Kamath, and Nair. Equality holds exactly when the variables are independent or form a doubly symmetric binary source. Combined with tensorization and data processing, the result also bounds mutual information between binary outputs from two correlated observation sequences, and this bound depends only on one pair's law when observation pairs are independent copies. ★★★★ Notable: The authors resolve the binary-pair conjecture, giving a tight bound on mutual information via the KL contraction coefficient and characterizing equality cases with supporting-tangent arguments.

entry.title: EviCast: Predicting Retrieval Benefits via Shared Response Calibration
entry.summary: EviCast: Forecasting Retrieval Gains Through Shared Response Calibration arXiv · Nov 2, 2026EviCast is a framework that forecasts whether retrieval-augmented generation will help a given generator, task, and retriever before running full large-scale experiments. It measures the generator's response to controlled evidence states once, then combines this with each retriever's evidence-state distribution to estimate end-to-end net utility and its 95% lower confidence bound. In evaluations on HotpotQA, MuSiQue, and a third dataset, it correctly decided most retrieval configurations while cutting diagnostic generation calls by 80%. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose forecasting RAG retrieval gains before execution via shared generator calibration, with a topology-aware variant; the abstract reports decisions across 14, 16, and 24 configuration

entry.title: Quantum state synthesis using an NP oracle
entry.summary: State Synthesis with an NP oracle arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This note presents a quantum algorithm that prepares an arbitrary state to inverse exponential precision in polynomial time using queries to an NP oracle, assuming direct access to entries of the state vector. The previous best upper bound on the required oracle complexity class was PP. The paper shows that any quantum algorithm with a P/poly oracle needs exponentially many queries, suggesting NP is the best possible upper bound. ★★★★ Notable: The authors improve the oracle complexity upper bound for arbitrary state preparation from PP to NP, and report an exponential query lower bound for P/poly oracles.

entry.title: Study Showing Prior Control Over Rewards Causally Changes Language-Model Plasticity
entry.summary: Prior Action Control Causally Alters Language-Model Plasticity arXiv · Nov 2, 2026Two copies of one language model, starting from identical weights, were trained on the same rewards, but one copy's rewards depended on its own answers while the other's were yoked to it. The copy with control learned a later new task faster, and this advantage persisted in a second experiment where both copies trained on identical, fixed answers. The authors also report that the advantage could be predicted from each copy's weights before the new task began. ★★★★ Notable: The authors adapt a learned-helplessness yoked design to test LLM plasticity, reporting paired experiments on Qwen3-0.6B and 1.7B with fixed-answer controls.

entry.title: Which Words a Model Fears: From a Refusal Direction to a Vocabulary-Wide Fear Lexicon
entry.summary: Which Words a Model Fears: From a Refusal Direction to a Vocabulary-Wide Fear Lexicon arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper studies whether aligned language models refuse requests partly based on which words appear in a prompt, independent of their meaning. The authors extract a refusal direction shared across prompts and words, and show that moving hidden states along it raises or lowers refusal monotonically with dose across eight models. Using this direction to score every vocabulary word, they validate the resulting ranking with two held-out tests. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend a refusal direction into a vocabulary-wide fear lexicon, showing single words can trigger refusal; validated across eight models with dose-response and two held-out tests.

entry.title: Achieving CSS code limits over Pauli channels with bounded graphical complexity
entry.summary: Achievability of CSS codes performance limits over Pauli channels under separate ML decoding with bounded graphical complexity arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper constructs ensembles of Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) quantum codes whose rates approach the CSS limit over memoryless Pauli channels under maximum-likelihood decoding, while keeping sparse, bounded-degree graphical representations. The approach separates parity-check density from graphical complexity by representing dense components through sparse concatenated factor graphs. The authors first analyze LDPC and LDGM component code combinations numerically, then introduce a second construction using concatenated LDPC, LDGM, and GIRA codes. They use the Miller-Burshtein framework to prove simultaneous reliability of the two CSS decoding components. ★★★★ Notable: The authors construct concatenated LDPC, LDGM and GIRA CSS ensembles that approach the hashing bound with bounded graphical complexity.

entry.title: Accessed, never disclosed: silent access to protected health information by medical AI agents
entry.summary: Accessed, never disclosed: Silent access to protected health information by medical artificial intelligence agents arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper examines whether medical AI agents access protected health information (PHI) tools even when a clinical task does not require patient identifiers. The authors embedded canaries in synthetic patient records and linked tool calls to canary exposure in final answers across five language models, four boundary levels, and seven attack frames. Three models invoked PHI tools unnecessarily, and the authors conclude that output-only evaluation cannot detect such silent access, so boundaries, pre-execution gates, and access-log audits are needed together. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce canary-based tracking of silent PHI access, showing output-only evaluation misses it, with experiments across five models, boundary levels, and attack frames.

entry.title: Language Model Capitulation Under Pushback: A Direction That Emerges With Scale
entry.summary: A Capitulation Direction Emerges With Scale and Is Causally Load-Bearing Where Validation Is Strong: Eight Models, Two Families, and Five Measurement Hazards arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper tests whether language models' tendency to abandon correct answers when users object corresponds to a linear direction in the residual stream, and whether that direction appears with scale. Across eight instruction-tuned models from 0.5B to 14B parameters in two families, under a pre-registered protocol, a direction clearing the validation gate appears at 7B, 8B and 14B. Ablating it in Qwen2.5-7B reduces answer reversals by 4.8 percentage points. ★★★★ Notable: The authors localise capitulation under pushback to a residual-stream direction and report a causal ablation reducing reversals by 4.8 points across eight pre-registered models.

entry.title: When the Text Is Silent: Memory Shortcuts in LLM Annotation
entry.summary: When the Text Is Silent: Memory Shortcuts and the Validity of LLM Annotation under Evidence Insufficiency arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper examines whether large language models, when annotating text, rely on what they already know about well-known people instead of the text itself. Using counterfactual texts built from 995 public figures and matched control names, the authors test three commercial LLMs and find that models never favor memory over conflicting text, but when evidence is absent, famous names raise the rates of inferred occupations, ages, and countries. The resulting labels are often factually correct about the namesake yet unsupported by the text, so they are methodologically invalid. ★★★★ Notable: The authors separate textual evidence from memorized knowledge, reporting memory shortcuts across 995 public figures, three commercial LLMs, and 121,594 prompts, plus mitigation trade-offs.

entry.title: Hinted Scaling Laws: Predicting Downstream Accuracy for Small Models Using Extra Hints
entry.summary: Hinted Scaling Laws arXiv · Nov 2, 2026Scaling laws forecast large model performance from smaller training runs, but they fail when small models score near zero on downstream benchmarks. This paper introduces hinted scaling laws, which use privileged information to create a range of easier benchmark versions so small models score above zero. Accuracy rises smoothly and predictably with hint level, and on the Delphi pretraining ladder the method forecasts GSM8K accuracy more accurately than a standard scaling law. Hinting also reduces the number of test examples needed to compare models.| ★★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce hinted scaling laws that keep small models above zero accuracy, reporting much lower GSM8K, AIME and HLE forecasting error across model families.

entry.title: Multiclass classification when only rare features are useful, and a screening method that works.
entry.summary: Multiclass Classification with Rare Useful Features: Fundamental Limits and the Optimality of Diversity Pursuit Higher Criticism Thresholding arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper studies high-dimensional multiclass classification where only a tiny fraction of features are useful and the number of classes may be large. It proposes Diversity Pursuit Higher Criticism Thresholding (DP-HCT), which applies a higher-criticism threshold to p-values from per-feature diversity tests such as one-way ANOVA. The authors show that whenever classification beyond chance is possible, DP-HCT with ANOVA and a simple class-mean similarity classifier achieves asymptotically perfect accuracy. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend rare-and-weak feature theory to multiclass, deriving a stricter phase transition with growing classes and DP-HCT optimality, validated on real benchmarks and simulations.

entry.title: Who Should Score the Cache? Mid-depth Layers Are the Best Judges of KV-cache Eviction
entry.summary: Who Should Score the Cache? Mid-Depth Layers Are the Best Judges of KV-Cache Eviction arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper studies which transformer layer's attention scores should decide which tokens to evict from the KV cache. Across twenty-one models, the depth of the scoring layer strongly affects long-context retrieval accuracy, with mid-depth layers (about 0.4 to 0.75 of depth) performing best. The authors propose selecting the scoring layer with calibration prompts that have known answers, which outperforms the default of each layer scoring its own cache on most models. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors ask which layer should score KV-cache tokens, report mid-depth layers peaking across twenty-one models, and compare against per-head SnapKV.

entry.title: Unified matrix framework for classifier discrimination, calibration and ranking
entry.summary: Discrimination, Calibration, and Ranking: A Unified Matrix Framework arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper proposes a single matrix-algebra framework covering the three pillars of classifier evaluation: discrimination, calibration and ranking. It extends an existing indicator-matrix approach for discrimination measures with deviation operators for a Calibration Framework and rank- and slice-dependent operators for a Ranking Framework, both sharing micro, macro and exemplar aggregation. The authors derive properties of Brier score, nDCG and AUC, and test the distinctions on two multilabel benchmarks. Many results are machine-checked in Lean 4. ★★★★ Notable: The authors unify discrimination, calibration and ranking in one matrix algebra, adding deviation and rank-dependent cell operators; results are partly Lean 4 machine-checked.

entry.title: Forecasting Earth surface change by predicting satellite image embeddings instead of raw spectral values
entry.summary: Forecasting Earth Surface Change in Embedding Space arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper proposes E²Forecast, a transformer-based model that forecasts Earth surface change in embedding space rather than raw spectral values, reducing the impact of clouds, shadows, and sensor noise. Its Gaussian branch predicts a mean and per-dimension uncertainty, while its rectified-flow branch generates forecast ensembles. On Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 benchmarks, forecasting embeddings halves cosine distance (0.20 to 0.10) and reduces overconfidence, and it raises F1 for anomalous change detection from 41.58 to 48.70 on a global benchmark. ★★★★ Notable: The authors forecast satellite embeddings instead of spectral values with a dual-branch transformer, reporting halved cosine distance across nine foundation models.

entry.title: Consolidating Multi-Agent Reasoning via Test-Time Training
entry.summary: Consolidating Reasoning with Test-Time Training arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper proposes TTT-Consolidate, which treats reasoning trajectories from multiple agents as adaptation data. Through test-time training, these trajectories are consolidated into a lightweight LoRA adapter, and a new solution is generated conditioned on that information. The method meta-learns consolidation via bi-level optimization and is built on the newly constructed OpenParallelThinking corpus of 12,810 math problems. On math and STEM benchmarks it outperforms the best aggregation baselines by up to 20 percentage points. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose consolidating multi-agent reasoning trajectories into a LoRA adapter via test-time training and bi-level meta-learning. The abstract reports up to 20-point gains over aggregation b

entry.title: Adaptive readout and decoding for diffusion driving VLA models by scene
entry.summary: Scene-Adaptive Readout and Decoding in Diffusion Driving VLAs arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper addresses the high inference cost of diffusion driving vision-language-action models, which rerun the backbone at every denoising stage. It proposes a scene-adaptive framework with a scene-conditioned readout mixture-of-experts that combines trajectory predictions from late-layer representations after one backbone pass, plus an adaptive decoding policy that adds refinement only when a scene requires it. Experiments on the Waymo E2E and nuScenes benchmarks report improved planning quality and up to a 6.0× end-to-end speedup on Waymo E2E. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose scene-adaptive readout and decoding for diffusion driving VLAs, reporting up to 6.0x speedup and RFS gains on Waymo E2E and nuScenes.

entry.title: Large Geometry Models as Priors for Fast Physics Pretraining
entry.summary: Large Geometry Models Are Priors For Fast Physics Pretraining arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper proposes Euler-Lagrange geometry pretraining, which derives pretraining targets from the flow's Euler-Lagrange equation using shape distance and normal information rather than designing them by hand. The authors present AREALS, a masked surface autoencoder pretrained self-supervised and sign-free on 61,822 raw meshes. It is evaluated on field reconstruction and fine-tuning data efficiency across DrivAerML, DrivAerNet++, WindsorML, and DoubleDelta wing datasets. ★★★★ Notable: The authors derive geometry pretraining targets from the Euler-Lagrange equation and propose AREALS, reporting reduced simulation needs across several aerodynamic datasets.

entry.title: Fragility vs. Hardness: Conditional Causal Difficulty for LLMs
entry.summary: Fragility Is Not Reducible to Hardness: Conditional Causal Difficulty for LLMs arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper treats LLM task difficulty as the causal effect of meaning-preserving rewrites, defining a conditional causal difficulty (CCD) over tasks the model can already solve. It introduces GlassGSM and GlassMATH, benchmarks that augment GSM8K and MATH with perturbation-built twin problems that raise fragility. A predictor called Frail estimates per-perturbation break probabilities and is compared against surface-feature and supervised baselines. ★★★★ Notable: The authors recast task difficulty as a conditional causal quantity and report comparisons with baselines on GlassGSM and GlassMATH.

entry.title: Paying for Fractional Error: Tight Constant-Round Approximation of Covering Problems
entry.summary: Paying for Fractional Error: Tight Constant-Round Approximation of Covering Problems with Short Broadcasts arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper presents a general framework for deterministic constant-round approximation of covering problems in sparse networks under the broadcast CONGEST model, where each vertex sends the same O(log n)-bit message to its neighbors. It combines a solver giving a (1+δ)-approximate solution to local covering linear programs and a rounding rule that turns an approximate fractional solution into an exact coefficient. For ordinary domination, it achieves a 2a+1 approximation against the fractional optimum under a minor edge-density assumption, which equals seven on planar graphs and matches a known lower bound. ★★★★ Notable: The authors combine a local covering LP solver with a rounding principle, reporting tight constant-round approximation coefficients matching lower bounds on planar graphs.

entry.title: LARK: Using Lean to formally verify GPU kernels written by AI
entry.summary: LARK: Lean-Assisted Reasoning for LLM-Generated GPU Kernels arXiv · Nov 2, 2026LARK is an agent framework that formally verifies GPU kernels generated by LLMs against their PyTorch reference implementations in Lean 4, rather than relying only on testing. Humans only need to verify the operator-level Lean semantics in advance, while LLM agents split each kernel into segments and prove each matches its PyTorch counterpart. On KernelCraft tasks, LARK fully verified 10 of 12 Level-1 kernels and all 5 Level-2 kernels. On 10 production kernels from open-source LLM serving frameworks, it verified 9 and found a new data race bug in the tenth. ★★★★ Notable: The authors formalize the GPU machine model in Lean 4 and use agents to prove kernel-to-PyTorch equivalence via segmentation; they report verifying 10 of 12 KernelCraft Level-1 kernels and finding one

entry.title: Switch-SWE: Can coding agents stay focused when switching between unfinished tasks?
entry.summary: Switch-SWE: Do Coding Agents Hold Focus When Switching Between Unfinished Tasks? arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper introduces Switch-SWE, a benchmark that tests whether coding agents can resume an earlier task after working on other unfinished tasks in the same repository. It includes 200 focus tasks from 19 Python repositories, evaluated in matched uninterrupted and interleaved sessions. Across 7 agents, interleaved work lowered focus-task resolution by an average of 11.5 percentage points. The authors also propose a context-management module that improves completion under task switching by 5.5 to 15.5 percentage points on OpenCode. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a benchmark of 200 focus tasks across 7 coding agents measuring resumption after same-repo task switching, plus a plug-in context module yielding 5.5 to 15.5 point gains.

entry.title: Optimal online learning in bilateral trade with interest
entry.summary: Optimal Online Learning in Bilateral Trade Through Interest arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper studies online learning in bilateral trade on platforms such as Uber, Airbnb, and eBay, where a platform posts prices to buyers and sellers and observes only whether trade occurs. It introduces global budget balance with interest, allowing trading profits and accrued interest to finance subsidies. The authors show that optimal regret against the best fixed common price drops from Θ̃(T^{3/4}) to Θ̃(T^{5/7}) as the interest rate grows, and that the optimal competitive ratio for the α-regret extension rises from 2 to 3. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce global budget balance with interest and report tight regret bounds in adversarial and i.i.d. valuation models across interest-rate regimes.

entry.title: "Seeing Why": Exact Evidence Maps for Quantum and Optical Image Classifiers
entry.summary: Seeing Why: Exact Evidence Maps for Quantum and Optical Image Classifiers arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper introduces Born evidence maps, which exactly split each class probability of quantum and all-optical image classifiers into contributions from the encoded image amplitudes. In simulation, four phase plates reach 72.3% accuracy on Caltech-10 colour photographs. On IBM's ibm_kingston hardware, 300 Caltech-10 test pictures were classified at 37.7% accuracy, against 10% by chance. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give an exact evidence decomposition for linear quantum and optical classifiers, equal to Integrated Gradients, and report hardware validation on IBM's ibm_kingston.

entry.title: Beyond Prompt Injection: The Tool Update Gap in LLM Agent Security
entry.summary: Beyond Prompt Injection: The Tool Update Gap in LLM Agent Security arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper examines how LLM agents that rely on external tools may keep trusting those tools after updates without re-verifying their safety, creating a supply-chain vulnerability. The authors introduce ETUDE, an attack that embeds malicious functionality into updates of initially benign tools while keeping their legitimate features, operating outside the LLM's context. Tested across three attack workloads and seven agentic frameworks, ETUDE achieved a 97.6% attack success rate with a 95.9% legitimate task completion rate, and existing defenses were found insufficient. ★★★★ Notable: The authors identify the tool update gap and propose ETUDE, reporting attack success and task completion across seven agentic frameworks.

entry.title: Launder-Bench: Can AI-driven rewrites of whole code repositories be detected?
entry.summary: Launder-Bench: Can Repository-Level Agentic Code Laundering Be Detected? arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper notes that coding agents can rewrite entire code repositories while preserving tested behavior, which challenges plagiarism detection, license auditing, and provenance tracing. The authors define repository-level agentic code laundering and introduce Launder-Bench, built from 282 real repositories, with pairwise detection and source-attribution tasks. Existing methods perform far from saturating the benchmark, revealing a gap between relative code similarity and source-specific provenance evidence. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a repository-level provenance benchmark for agentic rewriting, built from 282 repositories, reporting a gap between similarity and source evidence.

entry.title: Step-Zero Attack: Agent Safety Before Observability
entry.summary: Step-Zero Attack: Agent Safety Before Observability arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper argues that existing attacks and defenses for coding agents target the stage after content enters the model, while agents often must first process unknown files, network responses, or images to judge their safety, and that processing can itself cause harm. The authors call this initial processing "Step Zero" and test seven harnesses and six models. Most combinations exceeded a disk budget before the model saw any content, and the paper proposes a gate at the processing-primitive level that keeps extraction within budget. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce Step-Zero attacks, where harm occurs before the model reads content, testing seven harnesses and six models with a byte-counting gate defense.

entry.title: Continual learning in fully fine-tuned networks without replay, via hippocampus-inspired memory
entry.summary: Hippocampal consolidation without replay in fully fine-tuned networks arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper addresses catastrophic forgetting in neural networks that keep learning. It proposes a training-only hippocampal-style memory that indexes the input geometry of each group of synapses sharing an input, and limits how far each synapse can move in each direction. The authors report that this lets fully trainable networks keep learning without cross-task replay, a teacher model, or inference-time memory, across four architecture families and models up to 8 billion parameters. ★★★★ Notable: The authors index input geometry with a training-only hippocampal memory to limit synaptic movement, avoiding replay; they report gains across four architectures up to 8B parameters and 17.5 points ov

entry.title: RECEIPT: Fixing LLM Agents' Assumption That Tool Calls Finish
entry.summary: RECEIPT: Measuring and Repairing the Return Assumption of LLM Agents in Web Service Operations arXiv · Nov 1, 2026The paper examines the assumption that LLM agents' command-line tool calls return in bounded time with the requested action completed, showing that commands asking a question before acting can instead return success without doing the action or hang until timeout. The authors collected production and public agent trajectories, tested how eight widely used harnesses launch commands, and built two test sets, Litmus and Tripwire. They propose RECEIPT, which keeps input open, reads each process's waiting state from system calls, and reports it back to the agent, reducing false success claims by 73.5% across five LLMs. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report the first measurement of LLM agents' return assumption, proposing RECEIPT, which reads waiting state via system calls, evaluated on Litmus and Tripwire benchmarks.

entry.title: Watch Your Step: How Adam's Margin-Maximizing Bias Changes with Learning Rate Schedules
entry.summary: Watch Your Step: Adam's Margin Maximization Bias Depends on the Learning Rate Schedule arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper studies the implicit bias of Adam on homogeneous models for binary classification and its similarity to sign gradient descent. The authors show that this bias depends on the learning rate schedule, focusing on constant and weakly decaying schedules. In this regime, Adam has no trajectory-independent margin-maximization bias, but instead maximizes a trajectory-dependent weighted ℓ2 margin. In an intermediate regime, an ℓ∞ bias is proven under a gradient directional convergence condition. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show Adam's implicit bias depends on the learning rate schedule, characterizing it as trajectory-dependent weighted-ℓ2 margin maximization; theoretical results are reported for deep linear

entry.title: Does your long-horizon benchmark really test depth? Measuring and synthesizing depth in terminal tasks
entry.summary: Is Your Long-Horizon Benchmark Really Deep? Measuring and Synthesizing Depth in Terminal Tasks arXiv · Nov 1, 2026The paper examines long-horizon terminal tasks used to evaluate and train agents, arguing that turn counts and LLM-assigned difficulty labels do not reliably reflect task difficulty. It defines depth as the number of sequential turns required and audits 734 tasks from six existing datasets, finding that synthetic tasks mostly add work rather than depth. The authors propose DEPTH, a method that generates tasks segment by segment in a real software environment, producing 105 tasks that exceed the audited datasets in depth and work. Fine-tuning Qwen3-8B on runs from these tasks improves its performance on two terminal benchmarks. ★★★★ Notable: The authors measure terminal-task difficulty by sequential depth and propose segment-wise synthesis, reporting audits of six datasets and gains on two benchmarks after fine-tuning.

entry.title: Counting in Anonymous Directed Dynamic Networks: Exact Worst-Case Time and Per-Network Hardness
entry.summary: Computation in Anonymous Directed Dynamic Networks: Exact Worst-Case Termination Time and Network-Wise Intractability arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper studies the Counting problem in anonymous directed dynamic networks, where agents lack identifiers, some are leaders, and the population size is unknown. The authors give a distributed algorithm that makes every agent output the population size and halt after a round count that is tight in the worst case. They also show that, for a single fixed network, deciding whether an agent already has enough local information to determine the size is coNP-complete. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors give the exact worst-case round complexity of Counting in anonymous directed dynamic networks with a tight bound, and report coNP-completeness of per-network optimization.

entry.title: Scaling laws of partner feedback and convention rigidity in meta-learned multi-agent reinforcement learning
entry.summary: From Single-Agent Self-Discovery to Multi-Agent Adaptation: Scaling Laws of Partner Feedback and Convention Rigidity in Meta Reinforcement Learning Algorithms arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper studies whether meta-learned reinforcement learning algorithms, discovered automatically, keep improving when trained alongside teammates that also adapt, or whether they get trapped in brittle conventions. Over 1,800 runs in continuous robotics (VMAS) and discrete coordination (Overcooked), the authors report five laws of multi-agent adaptation. These cover evaluation illusions, feedback coupling, training length, cross-partner performance, and diagnostic signals. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report scaling laws for partner feedback and an evaluation illusion, tested over 1,800 runs in VMAS and Overcooked.

entry.title: How Chain-of-Thought Training Teaches Models to Reason: A Theory
entry.summary: How Does Chain-of-Thought Supervision Teach Models to Reason? A Theoretical Analysis arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper studies how training with chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision shapes a model's reasoning at inference time. The authors introduce an in-context weight prediction model trained on finite gradient descent trajectories for linear regression, and use high-dimensional asymptotic analysis to examine when long-horizon reasoning succeeds or fails. They distinguish two mechanisms of overthinking, error accumulation and error amplification, and report experiments with linear and multi-head softmax attention models that show these behaviors persist. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce an in-context weight prediction model and use high-dimensional asymptotics to show phase transitions in long-horizon reasoning, with experiments on attention models.

entry.title: Learned optical compression for single-pixel phase imaging
entry.summary: Learned optical compression for single-pixel quantitative phase imaging arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper presents a single-pixel quantitative phase imaging method that jointly optimizes a diffractive encoder and a digital neural decoder to compress reconstruction-relevant phase information into a compact measurement vector. A reconfigurable phase-modulation plane displays object-independent encoding patterns in sequence, each producing one scalar intensity measurement. Experiments at a visible wavelength achieve about 40-fold dimensional compression, using only 2.55% as many intensity measurements as reconstructed pixels. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose jointly optimized diffractive encoding and neural decoding for single-pixel quantitative phase imaging, reporting experiments on handwritten digits and grating phase objects with c

entry.title: How much random rotation improves GPTQ: sharp worst-case rate gaps at high rate
entry.summary: How Much Does Random Rotation Help GPTQ? Sharp Worst-Case Rate Gaps in the High-Rate Regime arXiv · Nov 1, 2026The paper studies the rate gap between GPTQ, a Cholesky-based Babai nearest-plane quantization algorithm, and WaterSIC in the high-rate, entropy-coded regime. It shows that after a Haar random rotation, the k-th pivot converges almost surely to a classical Lyapunov-exponent formula, which yields an asymptotic expression for the worst rotated rate gap. The authors conclude that rotation cannot in general replace waterfilling, though it nearly closes the gap on real layers. ★★★★ Notable: The authors characterize rotated GPTQ pivots via a classical Lyapunov-exponent formula, deriving a tight worst-case rate gap; they report validation on 96 Qwen3 and Llama-3.1 Hessians, mainly affectin

entry.title: Testing whether biological world models use actions, using design-based methods
entry.summary: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Design-Based Tests of Whether Biological World Models Use Actions arXiv · Nov 1, 2026Action-conditioned world models are often trained on randomized experiment data, and their dependence on actions is typically checked by removing actions and measuring the accuracy loss. The paper shows that under autocorrelated designs such diagnostics can report action effects that do not exist. It proposes a conditional randomization test written as an e-value and analyzes how pooled scores over many sites sharing one action sequence can amplify small model errors. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show action-perturbation diagnostics yield false effects and propose design-based e-value tests with pooling amplification, reported on synthetic and optogenetic ERK experiments.

entry.title: Near-optimal √K regret for online learning in games where opponent actions are hidden
entry.summary: Near-Optimal √K-Regret for Online Learning in Uninformed Markov Games arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper studies online learning in two-player Markov games where the learner cannot observe the opponent's actions and the opponent may use any unknown policy in each episode. The authors present an algorithm that achieves Õ(H^{3/2}S√(AK)) empirical Nash-value regret against arbitrary opponent policies, settling an open question about whether the √K rate holds in the worst case. The method combines global and local planning, coordinating them to control the gap between local loss estimates and the total loss of the executed policy. ★★★★ Notable: The authors resolve an open question on worst-case √K regret, proposing an algorithm combining global and local planning with an H^{3/2}S√(AK) bound.

entry.title: BanglishDepYT: Depression detection in native Bengali social media
entry.summary: BanglishDepYT: Depression Detection in Native Bengali Social Media with Emotion-Preserving Preprocessing and Domain-Adaptive Pretraining arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper introduces BanglishDepYT, a Bengali depression dataset collected natively from YouTube, with 191,000 unlabeled comments and 1,000 dual-annotated samples. The authors propose EPH, an emotion-preserving preprocessing method that keeps emoticons, Banglish tokens, and negations, and show it markedly improves performance on informal text. They also apply domain-adaptive pretraining to SahajBERT, which achieves the highest mean F1 and MCC, and use LLM-assisted pseudo-labeling with semi-supervised training to expand annotations. ★★★★ Notable: The authors combine emotion-preserving preprocessing with domain-adaptive pretraining, reporting comparisons and significance tests on native Bengali YouTube comments.

entry.title: Sonny-ENS: a machine-learning ensemble weather forecasting model explained
entry.summary: Sonny-ENS: demystifying machine-learning ensemble weather forecasting arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper presents Sonny-ENS, an ensemble of three 68.9-million-parameter neural networks using Monte Carlo dropout, trained on the continuous ranked probability score in 2.7 A40 GPU-days. On 2022 data, it beats the ECMWF ensemble on 96% of 570 targets and has 8.3% lower mean CRPS at lead times of 1 to 10 days. The authors also find that dropout adds uncertainty mainly in the tropics, and that forecast spread tracks baroclinic instability in the atmosphere. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors report that a dropout-based ML ensemble trained in 2.7 GPU-days beats ENS and GenCast on 2022 targets, with ablations and sparse-autoencoder analysis of spread sources.

entry.title: Evaluating diffusion video inpainting by how recoverable each hidden pixel is
entry.summary: Recoverability-Aware Evaluation of Diffusion Video Inpainting and Object Removal arXiv · Nov 1, 2026Video inpainting for object removal is usually scored over the whole hole, which mixes copying visible background with generating new content. The paper proposes recoverability-stratified evaluation, using a point tracker to label each hole pixel by whether and how far away it is observed, and introduces training-free evidence-guided sampling (EGS) that blends tracked colors into a video diffusion remover. On DAVIS, the perceptual advantage of diffusion removers over flow propagation shrinks where content is visible a few frames away, and EGS closes 43% and 56% of the gap to a copy reference on held-out DAVIS when colors come from clean-video tracks. With tracks computed on the masked input, the method gave no gain on MiniMax-Remover and a loss on ROSE. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose recoverability-stratified evaluation and training-free evidence-guided sampling, reporting on DAVIS, real paired captures, and a pre-registered confirmation on two removers.

entry.title: Principled human-AI collaboration for deciding which AI outputs can skip review
entry.summary: Principled Human-AI Collaboration in Agentic Workflows arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper presents a statistical framework for deciding which AI-generated answers can be released without human review. Experts evaluate selected outputs before deployment, and their judgments calibrate the verifier threshold and number of attempts, without modifying the generator or verifier. In a MultiHiertt financial question-answering case study, the automation rate rose from 2.50% to 24.17% while the error rate among released outputs stayed around 1.20%. ★★★★ Notable: The authors calibrate verifier thresholds and attempt counts from expert evaluations, giving finite-sample error control and a minimax lower bound. The paper reports automation gains on MultiHiertt fi

entry.title: Why Vision-Language Models Can Read Text in Images but Still Fail to Use It
entry.summary: VLMs Read Aloud: The Gap Between Recognizing and Using Visual Text arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper finds that vision-language models can transcribe text in images word for word yet still fail to answer questions from it, a gap the authors call the read-use gap. Recognizing and using visual text need different resolutions, and putting the evidence into words narrows the gap. The authors propose ALOUD, which uses visual resolution to find and recognize evidence and language tokens to use it, roughly doubling a frozen model's accuracy on long documents compressed 5x and 10x. ★★★★ Notable: The authors identify a read-use gap in VLMs and propose ALOUD, reporting roughly doubled accuracy on compressed long documents versus a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B and comparisons with several methods.

entry.title: Causal optimal-transport attention with positional priors for length extrapolation
entry.summary: Causal Optimal-Transport Attention: Positional Priors and Length Extrapolation arXiv · Nov 1, 2026The paper studies how causal masking affects optimal-transport attention and characterizes the positional prior it induces, showing attention is diluted as context grows for a fixed balancing strength. Preregistered experiments with 25M- and 100M-parameter language models report better long-context loss extrapolation than softmax. An explicit distance-bias method, CABLE, is reported to outperform RoPE with YaRN at three training lengths. ★★★★ Notable: The authors analyze a causal unbalanced OT attention, its positional prior, and report preregistered 25M and 100M model experiments against RoPE with YaRN.

entry.title: Study on whether data exchange between competing firms can remain stable
entry.summary: The Stability of Data Exchange in Competitive Markets arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper examines whether competing firms can exchange data in a stable way when their predictive performance affects market share. It models n firms sharing parts of their datasets and uses core stability as the solution concept. The authors show that a core-stable exchange always exists in fully rational markets, but may fail to exist under logit-style demand. They also show that equal sharing of market-share revenue within coalitions restores existence of a core-stable exchange. ★★★★ Notable: The authors formalize core stability of data exchange among competing firms, give existence and non-existence results under two demand models, and report simulations.

entry.title: Privacy sensitivity inflation from cross-record precision routing in quantized fine-tuning
entry.summary: Sensitivity Inflation from Cross-Record Precision Routing in Private Quantized Fine-Tuning arXiv · Nov 1, 2026The paper shows that LLM.int8, used in private fine-tuning of frozen quantized language models, routes outlier activation columns based on a batch-wide union, so one record can change how other records are computed and exceed the standard sensitivity bound. The authors bound this sensitivity inflation and propose a record-isolation contract along with record-owned precision dispatch that uses the same matrix multiplications as batched LLM.int8. Audits of the native CUDA stack find records exceeding the bound in practice. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show LLM.int8 cross-record precision routing inflates DP-SGD sensitivity, propose a record-isolation contract and dispatch, and report native CUDA experiments.

entry.title: Backdoor attack on vision-language models that hides during full-token audits
entry.summary: Context-Shielded Backdoor Attack against Large Vision-Language Models arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper studies how inference-time visual-token compression in large vision-language models affects backdoor attacks. The authors find that surrounding clean visual tokens suppress an embedded trigger at full length, while token pruning removes that context and activates the backdoor. They propose StripWake, a projector-only backdoor that stays dormant under full-token auditing but activates across unseen compressors. On LLaVA-1.5-7B, it achieves 0.4% full-token attack success rate and 94.0%-99.7% under compression. ★★★★ Notable: The authors identify context stripping and propose a projector backdoor dormant under full tokens but active after compression, reporting results on LLaVA-1.5-7B across nine compressors.

entry.title: How much approximate equilibria can change the total cost of selfish routing
entry.summary: How Much Can Approximate Equilibria Change the Social Cost of Selfish Routing? arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper studies approximate Nash equilibria in nonatomic congestion games, where each player's cost may be up to 1+ε times the minimum available cost. It compares the social cost of these ε-approximate equilibria with that of exact Nash equilibria. For degree-d polynomial latencies, it gives tight bounds on the relative change in social cost, showing that for small ε both the largest reduction and increase in general congestion games are Θ(√(dε)). On series-parallel networks of depth h, the largest relative reduction is Θ(hε), which separates these networks from general games. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give tight bounds on social cost change for approximate equilibria with polynomial latencies, separating general congestion games from series-parallel networks.

entry.title: GSLM2: Learning Speech Structure from Multiple Streams of Discrete Units
entry.summary: GSLM2: Multi-Stream Speech Representation Learning and Generative Spoken Language Modeling arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper presents GSLM2, a generative spoken language model that learns language structure purely from speech. Its SpidR 2.0 encoder produces discrete speech units at multiple levels of abstraction, and a multi-stream model jointly models them. Scaled up to 6M hours of data and 6.5B parameters, it improves linguistic competence and narrows the gap with text-based models. The training code and model checkpoints are open-sourced. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors propose multi-stream discrete speech units with a joint autoregressive model, reporting gap reductions on sWuggy, sBLIMP, and tSC up to 6M hours and 6.5B parameters.

entry.title: What a safety label measures: auditing multimodal LLM safety benchmarks
entry.summary: What Does a Safety Label Measure? Auditing Situational-Safety Benchmarks for Multimodal LLMs arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper audits situational-safety benchmarks for multimodal large language models, which label scenes SAFE or UNSAFE and score model answers against those labels. The authors propose a Benchmark Card with seven measured fields to show whether scores come from the scene, the request, or benchmark design, and fill it for six benchmarks. They find that some benchmarks leak the label through non-scene signals, such as image file size on one chat benchmark. They also introduce the Spot-Stop decomposition, which splits the gap between ranking and labelling performance into threshold, overlap, and within-pair order components. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose Benchmark Card and Spot-Stop decomposition, auditing six situational-safety benchmarks for label leakage across fourteen open MLLMs.

entry.title: Blind spots of detection: attacks on watchdogs in distributed LLM inference
entry.summary: The Blind Spots of Detection: Adversarial Perturbation Attacks against Watchdogs in Distributed LLM Inference arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper examines how a malicious node in decentralized large language model inference can sabotage generation while staying within the numerical tolerance used for verification. The authors introduce Hush-Up, which adds adversarial perturbations to output activations to raise the end-of-sequence token probability and force premature termination. The paper reports that this attack can also cause existing defenses to miss the sabotage or wrongly blame honest workers. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a stealthy attack that uses adversarial perturbations within benign error bounds to halt distributed LLM inference and evade watchdog detection across models and benchmarks.

entry.title: Infinite Worlds from One Example: Sharing Randomness in Local Generators
entry.summary: Infinite Worlds from One Example: What Local Generators Must Share arXiv · Nov 1, 2026The paper studies local generators that create unbounded game worlds on demand, with every small window required to come from a single example, as in Wave Function Collapse. It shows that a generator applying one position-independent rule to independent randomness at each cell cannot be both exactly valid and faithful to the example's statistics when constraints vary across the example. It gives a finitely checkable condition for exact validity using seed-based row types and position modulo a period, and tests it on 52 public Wave Function Collapse examples and 27 from other implementations. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show local generators need shared randomness, prove independent randomness cannot be both exactly valid and faithful, and give a matching 1/r lower bound.

entry.title: Leap-VLA: Fast Robot Control Driven by a Slowly Updated Vision-Language Model
entry.summary: Leap-VLA: High-Rate Robot Control from a Low-Rate VLM Backbone arXiv · Oct 31, 2026This paper presents a vision-language-action model that runs a large vision-language model at low frequency to produce cached semantic context, which is reused across control steps. A flow-matching action expert runs at high frequency, combining this cache with a fresh visual stream from a compact encoder. Training explicitly covers cache age, so the policy remains effective as the cached context becomes stale. On LIBERO benchmark suites, the deployed policy reaches success rates close to a frequency-matched anchor. ★★★★ Notable: The authors decouple a low-rate VLM cache from a high-rate flow-matching action expert, conditioning on cache age; the paper reports asynchronous deployment results on LIBERO suites.

entry.title: Optimal Learning in Fairness-Aware Contextual Bandits: A theoretical study of learning with fairness constraints in sequential decisions
entry.summary: Optimal Learning in Fairness-Aware Contextual Bandits arXiv · Oct 31, 2026This paper studies contextual bandits under a global Lipschitz fairness constraint, requiring individuals with similar contexts to receive similar action distributions. The authors show the constraint creates a randomisation region near the decision boundary and quantify the population-level cost of fairness. They propose a lazy fair greedy algorithm and a lazy polyhedral UCB algorithm, both satisfying fairness at every round, with regret of order O(√T + T^{(d-2)/(d-1)}) up to poly-logarithmic factors. A matching minimax lower bound establishes optimality, and experiments support the theoretical findings. ★★★★ Notable: The authors characterise optimal fair policies under Lipschitz fairness, give regret bounds with a matching minimax lower bound, and propose two algorithms tested experimentally.

entry.title: SNAPPerf: A software-aware model that predicts configurable software performance without retraining
entry.summary: SNAPPerf: Software-Aware Tabular Foundation Model for Retraining-Free Performance Prediction of Configurable Systems arXiv · Oct 31, 2026Software configuration options strongly affect runtime, memory, and energy use, but their combinations are too numerous to benchmark exhaustively. SNAPPerf is a tabular foundation model pretrained once on synthetic data that predicts performance from a few measured configurations used as context, with no per-system training or tuning. Across 39,866 configurations from 12 real-world systems, it reduces prediction error by 38% over the prior state of the art and by 25% over the best general-purpose tabular foundation model at the same measurement budget. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a pretrained tabular foundation model that predicts configurable software performance from few measurements without retraining, reporting gains over prior methods on 12 real system

entry.title: The covering radius of the nine-variable first-order Reed-Muller code is 242
entry.summary: The covering radius of the first-order Reed-Muller code in nine variables is 242 arXiv · Oct 31, 2026This paper proves that the covering radius of the binary first-order Reed-Muller code RM(1,9) is exactly 242, equivalently that the maximum nonlinearity of a nine-variable Boolean function is 242. The proof combines a one-point rigidity theorem with spectral and computational exclusion of the two larger candidate nonlinearities. Together with a known construction attaining nonlinearity 242, these arguments establish the result. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors prove the covering radius of RM(1,9) equals 242, combining a one-point rigidity theorem with spectral and computational exclusion of larger candidates.

entry.title: Is Random Sampling Enough? Stable, Low-Cost Benchmark Compression with BestRand
entry.summary: Random Is Almost Enough? Stable and Low-Cost Benchmark Compression via BestRand arXiv · Oct 31, 2026This paper studies how to evaluate models on a small subset of a benchmark instead of the full set, cutting evaluation cost. The authors derive an analytical approximation of the error distribution when estimating full-benchmark scores from a subset, finding that most subsets have small errors while a few have large ones. They propose BestRand, which keeps the efficiency of random sampling while reducing this high-error tail, and validate it on over 70 text, multimodal, and agent benchmarks. ★★★★ Notable: The authors derive a long-tailed error approximation for subset-based benchmark estimation and propose BestRand, reporting validation on 70+ text, multimodal, and agent benchmarks plus VLA evaluation.

entry.title: Noise stability on the hypercube at order 7/8: a study of how balanced Boolean functions keep their values steady under random noise.
entry.summary: Noise Stability on the Hypercube: Order 7/8 arXiv · Oct 31, 2026The paper studies the alpha-stability of balanced Boolean functions on the discrete hypercube, defined via the Boolean noise operator for exponents between 0 and 1. Using asymmetric Hellinger kernel estimates recently established by OpenAI, it proves that dictator functions minimize the 7/8-stability in every dimension and at every correlation, and are the only minimizers at interior correlations. It follows that dictators minimize alpha-stability for 7/8 to 1, maximize it for 1 to 2, and maximize one-sided Shannon entropy stability. The result resolves a conjecture of Li and Médard and strengthens the Courtade–Kumar conjecture in the balanced case. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report proving dictators minimize the 7/8-stability at all correlations, resolving a Li–Médard conjecture and strengthening Courtade–Kumar in the balanced setting.

entry.title: Checking crop maps fairly when field labels are biased
entry.summary: Crop Mapping Evaluation under Sampling Bias arXiv · Oct 31, 2026Crop maps used for food security and farm policy are usually checked against field labels that cluster near roads and skip hard-to-reach parcels. The paper proposes a weighted prediction-powered inference method that uses satellite embeddings to estimate performance across the whole mapped region. In tests across five European regions with complete reference labels, simulated collection practices produced gaps of up to 0.20 macro-F1, and the method reduced the largest error across regions to 0.07. ★★★★ Notable: The authors apply weighted prediction-powered inference to estimate crop-map deployment gaps, validating on five European regions with complete reference labels.

entry.title: Tight stochastic sequential covers for general VC classes with unknown i.i.d. features
entry.summary: Tight Stochastic Sequential Covers for General VC Classes with Unknown i.i.d. Features arXiv · Oct 31, 2026This paper studies hybrid online learning, where features are stochastic and labels are adversarial, with an unknown feature distribution. The authors show that any binary class with finite VC dimension d admits a distribution-blind exact cover with log-size O(d log T + log(1/δ)), matching the worst-case lower bound. The construction uses a new local cube weight that counts Boolean subcubes incident to each realizable trace, and splits probability mass unevenly accordingly. The paper also shows that this binary phenomenon does not extend to pseudo-dimension, since a fixed pseudo-dimension-one sigmoid class needs Ω(log² T) bits for uniform sequential approximation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce local cube weights with uneven splitting, giving a tight log-size cover for general VC classes matching the stated lower bound.

entry.title: The Long Con: Web Fraud Attacks That Build Trust Before Exploiting Coding Agents
entry.summary: The Long Con on the Web: Earn-then-Exploit Fraud Attacks against Coding Agents arXiv · Oct 31, 2026The paper introduces EtE (Earn-then-Exploit), an attack in which a malicious website first gives verifiably helpful assistance to build trust, then issues instructions that exceed intended operational boundaries. Tested across 56 organizational environments and three coding agents, it achieved an average scene-level attack success rate of 71.4%. The authors also show that agents rely on previously helpful web sources in a trust-like way, which raises their susceptibility to later malicious instructions, and they propose action-authorization separation (AAS), which reduces attack success to 0% while keeping 100% task completion. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose an earn-then-exploit attack framework and report a 71.4% scene-level success rate across 56 environments and three coding agents.

entry.title: Adversarial Robustness Is Not Zero-Day Generalization: Testing Flow-Based Intrusion Detectors on Corrected CIC-IDS2017
